articles.title: NCSC Chief Warns of Imminent AI Ransomware Threat to UK Critical Infrastructure - Infosecurity Magazine
articles.summary: NCSC Chief Warns of Imminent AI Ransomware Threat to UK Critical Infrastructure  Infosecurity Magazine
articles.full_text:
AI-powered malware is strongly expected to feature in ransomware attacks on the UK’s critical national infrastructure by 2028, the country’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has warned.
The country faces “a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents,” NCSC CEO Richard Horne said during the launch event for the agency’s annual State of the Cyber Nation report in London, on November 3.
Horne said this heightened threat is supercharged by the use of AI, whose impact “will be felt by us all, whether you and your organization choose to harness it or not.”
The report warned that AI-powered malicious software is “highly likely” to be used in cyber-attacks conducted by financially motivated hackers against the UK’s power stations, airports and hospitals by 2028.
It also warned that nation states including Russia and China will routinely use AI in their cyber activity to achieve their geopolitical goals.
Yet, Horne emphasized that AI-based threats have not fundamentally revealed anything new.
The risk that looms is “not because AI has invented new ways to attack us,” he argued, but “because vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long can now be discovered and exploited at a scale that was once unimaginable.”
He pointed to “far too many organizations” relying on “tech on the cheap.”
“End-of-life systems kept running for just one more year, well-needed upgrades pushed back, as a 'cost efficiency' and technology providers failing to invest in security by design and default,” Horne outlined.
“We have installed technology then failed to invest in it throughout its lifecycle. Granted access where it was convenient rather than where it was necessary. Procured services based solely on their price without asking whether the technologies and operations underpinning them was resilient or secure. And failed to put in place the monitoring needed to detect when things go wrong,” he added.
UK Government Announces New Cybersecurity Investments
The best recent example, Horne said, is the threat of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. He noted that his agency has issued 110,000 proactive notifications and Early Warning alerts to UK organizations in response to the PHP vulnerabilities.
He also welcomed recent news that the British government has invested £60m ($80.4m) into developing the first phase of a national Cyber Shield, including a £25m ($33.5m) Challenge Fund supporting UK AI and cyber security innovators, and £70m ($93.8m) for a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre.
These announcements, made on October 24, come alongside an additional £120m ($160.8m) investment in the AI Security Institute (AISI) and the establishment of new AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence, ran by the NCSC in Manchester to provide world leading AI security expertise within government.
The government has also committed £40m ($53.6m) to establishing a National Agentic Security Unit to monitor and respond to uncontrolled AI bots, alongside a further £24m ($32.1m) to strengthen public-sector cyber defenses using advanced AI technology.
Alongside these investments, Cyber Security Minister, Baroness Lloyd, announced in a speech at the NCSC Annual Review event that the UK government is offering a 75% discount on Cyber Essentials certification for micro, small and medium-sized businesses, bringing the cost down to between £80 ($107) and £125 ($168), plus VAT.
More than 230 businesses have also signed up to the government's Cyber Resilience Pledge, which will allow participating organizations to refer SMEs in their supply chains for free Cyber Essentials certification, with selected businesses also receiving support from a free cyber security advisor.
The government also announced 14 new Software Security Ambassadors, including Fortinet, Thales, Capgemini and Zscaler, which will work with the government to promote secure software development and encourage wider adoption of its Software Security Code of Practice.
A “Moment of Choice” for UK Organizations
Horne said UK organizations and at “a moment of choice” and urged them to “reckon with the current state of their cybersecurity” as new technologies like AI will expose vulnerabilities, failings and underinvestment at an unprecedented speed and scale in the years ahead.
The NCSC report also suggested that the UK is at a point of “enormous consequence” for cybersecurity and that organizations must make use of the tools, standards and frameworks that already exist and are evidenced to protect them from conventional and AI-powered cyber-attacks.
"We can be a nation where leaders of all organizations actively choose to invest with urgency and where all organizations make security and resilience a fundamental requirement, not an afterthought. The collective result would be a source of enduring national strength for us all,” Horne said in his speech.
He added that failing to make these choices will result in leaders “having to look their investors, shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, in the eye and explain, when food isn’t on shelves, lights aren’t on, businesses have gone under.”
Commenting on the report, Anthony Young, CEO at UK-based critical infrastructure security provider Bridewell, stressed that the NCSC’s two-year warning “feels generous.”
“AI is already helping attackers, and vulnerability discovery is accelerating faster than many organizations can test and deploy patches. There is no time to wait when so many of the weaknesses attackers can exploit are already there, highlighting the recent attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems are a good example of this and “an extension of the problems we have seen for years with internet-connected CCTV and heating or ventilation systems.”
“Organizations cannot assume that insurance will resolve the consequences of an attack when essential services are disrupted. Cyber Essentials matters because so many attacks still exploit basic weaknesses, and leaving those weaknesses in place makes life too easy for everyone from amateur hackers to nation-state attackers. We’ve spent 25 years telling organisations to get the basics right. AI is making it harder for them to get away with ignoring that advice,” Young added.
The warnings come as the UK government is taking action through the introduction of the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill and the forthcoming National Cyber Action Plan to strengthen the UK's defenses.

articles.title: NCSC Warns AI Could Accelerate Ransomware Attacks on Critical Infrastructure - CyberSecurityNews
articles.summary: NCSC Warns AI Could Accelerate Ransomware Attacks on Critical Infrastructure  CyberSecurityNews
articles.full_text:
The UK’s National Cyber Security Center handled 80 nationally significant cyber incidents during its latest reporting year, warning that artificial intelligence is making attacks faster, cheaper and easier to carry out. Its 2026 Annual Review records 1,831 attack reports, with 337 incidents requiring support from its Incident Management Team.
The review covers 1 September 2025 to 31 August 2026, marking the NCSC’s tenth year as part of GCHQ. Published on November 3, the NCSC Annual Review 2026 warns that AI is increasing pressure on organizations still struggling to fix known security weaknesses.
The 80 nationally significant incidents represent a subset of the 337 cases that needed NCSC support, not the total number of cyber attacks across the UK. Alongside its response work, the agency notified 8,500 organizations of events indicating suspected system compromise through its Early Warning service.
The NCSC cautions against reading incident totals as a simple measure of whether threats are rising or falling. Reporting levels vary, major incidents can influence annual figures, and early alerts may prevent smaller compromises from developing into cases requiring national support. Response complexity also differs widely between incidents.
That context matters when comparing this review with earlier reporting on nationally significant UK cyber attacks. A lower incident count does not, by itself, prove that organizations face less risk or that the impact of individual attacks has decreased.
AI Could Accelerate Ransomware
The report’s central finding is not that attackers have abandoned established techniques. Instead, AI is helping them research targets, produce convincing social engineering messages, discover software flaws, and develop exploit code more efficiently. Skilled operators currently gain the greatest benefit because they can check results and correct mistakes.
The agency’s incident management findings draw an important line between observed activity and future risks. Its responders have begun seeing attackers use AI tools, but none of those observed uses enabled a new class of attack. Existing security controls therefore remain directly relevant.
Across the large organizations covered by its incident data, 88% of incidents involved four initial access routes: public-facing applications, phishing, valid accounts and external remote services. These findings show why exposed software, stolen login details and poorly protected remote access remain immediate concerns, even as AI capabilities improve.
Human involvement also remains important. The NCSC assesses that attackers will continue using AI mainly to improve existing operations rather than routinely handing complete attacks to autonomous systems. Operators still need to direct tools, validate findings and adapt when an approach fails.
The review warns that AI-powered malware is highly likely to feature in a ransomware attack against UK critical national infrastructure between now and 2028. This is a forecast, not confirmation that such an incident has already happened.
Its assessment of threats to the UK also expects China, Russia and other states to routinely use AI cyber capabilities by 2028. The likely result is an increase in the speed and scale of sophisticated operations against UK targets.
Businesses face risks from their own AI adoption too. The report warns that employees using unapproved AI services can expose sensitive company information and leave employers unable to track how that data is handled. Earlier coverage of CISA and NCSC secure AI development guidance explains why security must be considered throughout an AI system’s life.
For defenders, AI-assisted flaw discovery could create a growing workload of security updates. The NCSC urges organisations to prepare for a “patch wave” by improving their ability to deploy fixes quickly, frequently and across suppliers. Not every AI-discovered flaw will be exploitable, but delays can give attackers opportunities.
The immediate priorities remain practical: maintain an accurate view of systems, patch exposed services, control account access, protect backups and rehearse incident response. The review also supports wider passkey adoption and better understanding of supplier dependencies. These measures address the access routes responders continue to encounter.
AI can also help defenders identify weaknesses, review alerts, and support faster response. However, automated actions need clear limits and human oversight to avoid disruption. The challenge is turning that potential into reliable protection while replacing aging technology and consistently applying the basic controls that many organizations still lack today.

articles.summary: Russia confirms new Ukraine peace talks as Melania Trump prepares to host ceasefire meeting  CNBCZelensky speaks with US envoys ahead of trilateral talks  The HillUS to mediate new round of negotiations to end Russia-Ukraine war  PoliticoUkraine’s Zelenskyy hopes Abu Dhabi talks will open path to Putin meeting  Al JazeeraKremlin confirms trilateral Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi next week  Reuters
articles.full_text:
Russia on Tuesday confirmed that peace talks with Ukraine and the U.S. will go ahead next week in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, while also signaling that a meeting between Presidents Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping to end the conflict was on the table.
Putin aide Vladimir Medinsky will serve as Moscow's chief negotiator at the talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on a conference call, according to Reuters.
Separately, first lady Melania Trump will bring Russian and Ukrainian representatives to the White House to discuss the local ceasefire in Kherson, the White House said Tuesday.
Monday saw the end of a six-day ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky and surrounding areas in the Kherson region to allow for evacuation of residents, in a pause of hostilities that the White House said was brokered by the first lady.
Ukraine on Monday accused Russia of using the ceasefire to reinforce its military positions in the city.
The first lady's summit on Thursday will be "an extraordinary moment in American history," the White House said, but did not name the representatives who will attend. Melania Trump will deliver remarks on the Oleshky ceasefire at 11 a.m. ET on Thursday, it added.
Peskov also said Tuesday the Kremlin hopes to finalize plans for a trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, the U.S. and China in the coming days. The comments follow earlier reports that these countries were planning to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, without Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the table.
Zelenskyy has said that any negotiations over Ukraine's future must include Kyiv.
"It can be acceptable only when we are at the table of negotiations," he said on Oct. 20, adding that he had discussed the proposal of a three-way meeting between the U.S., China and Russia to negotiate an end to the nearly five-year full-scale war. "Nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine," he said.
Tensions between the U.S. and Ukraine have mounted over recent weeks amid continued strikes between Moscow and Kyiv, including on civilian and energy targets.
A series of moves by the Trump administration in October raised questions about Washington's reliability as Kyiv's most important military partner.
Tuesday's announcement follows U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff saying late Monday that Washington will mediate Ukraine-Russia peace talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11, focusing on security arrangements, de-escalation and humanitarian issues.
Witkoff also said that U.S. negotiators will meet European and NATO officials in Brussels this week to discuss postwar security guarantees and Ukraine's reconstruction.

articles.title: EU defense chief warns Russian military spending nears European levels - Yeni Şafak English
articles.summary: EU defense chief warns Russian military spending nears European levels  Yeni Şafak English
articles.full_text:
Andrius Kubilius says Moscow's military budget will match Europe's combined expenditure next year in purchasing power parity terms, warning that Russian military potential is not diminishing as the US pivots to the Indo-Pacific.
Berlin Security Conference
EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius warned on Tuesday that Russian military spending will nearly match Europe's combined defense expenditure next year when measured in purchasing power parity terms. Speaking at the Berlin Security Conference, he stated: "Russian military potential is not diminishing." He added: "If you calculate in purchasing power parity terms, Russia is ready to spend almost the same amount that we Europeans are going to spend next year, around €500 billion ($559 billion)."
Transatlantic priorities
Kubilius stressed the need to strengthen the European pillar within NATO as Washington shifts its strategic focus toward the Indo-Pacific region. "Americans will pay more and more attention towards the Indo-Pacific region. And that is what we need to have in mind when we are talking about what capabilities we need to develop here on the European continent," he said.
He noted that Europeans must invest in addressing capability gaps to ensure continental security remains robust amid the US pivot. The commissioner emphasized that new investments should focus on areas where allies currently lack sufficient capacity.
EU-NATO relationship
The commissioner reiterated that Brussels' plans to bolster defense capabilities do not represent an alternative to the Atlantic alliance. "There really is no competition between the European Union and NATO. NATO is a military might, EU is an economic power. And our task is how to combine these two strengths into European defense capabilities which should deter Russia," Kubilius said.
The remarks come amid ongoing debates within the 32-member alliance over burden-sharing and strategic autonomy.

articles.title: UK Warns AI-Powered Ransomware Threat to Critical Infrastructure by 2028 - KuCoin
articles.summary: UK Warns AI-Powered Ransomware Threat to Critical Infrastructure by 2028  KuCoin
articles.full_text:
The National Cyber Security Centre says an AI-assisted attack on critical systems is highly likely within three years.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre, part of intelligence agency GCHQ, has issued a stark warning about the future of ransomware. It says an AI-powered attack on critical national infrastructure is highly likely by 2028. The warning covers sectors such as energy, water, transport and healthcare, all considered essential to public life.
According to reporting from Cryptopolitan and Decrypt, the NCSC's assessment centers on how artificial intelligence is changing the economics of cybercrime. Attackers can now use AI tools to automate reconnaissance, craft convincing phishing messages, and identify software vulnerabilities faster than before. This lowers the skill barrier for launching sophisticated attacks and speeds up the pace at which they can be executed.
Ransomware has already been a persistent threat to UK institutions. Hospitals, local councils and private firms have all faced disruptive attacks in recent years, often involving data encryption and extortion demands. What the NCSC is flagging now is a qualitative shift. AI does not just make existing attack methods faster. It potentially enables entirely new approaches that are harder to detect using current defenses.
Critical infrastructure is a particular concern because disruption there carries consequences beyond financial loss. An attack on an energy grid or water system can affect public safety directly. Security agencies have long treated these sectors as priority targets for defense precisely because the fallout from a successful breach extends far beyond the targeted organization.
The warning fits into a broader pattern of government agencies worldwide grappling with dual-use AI technology. The same tools that help defenders detect anomalies and respond to threats can also be repurposed by attackers to probe for weaknesses. This arms-race dynamic has become a recurring theme in cybersecurity policy discussions over the past two years.
The NCSC's timeline of 2028 suggests officials believe there is a window to prepare, rather than an immediate crisis. That framing is likely intended to prompt investment in defenses now, including AI-aware detection systems, workforce training and updated incident response plans. Governments have historically used forward-looking threat assessments to justify funding and regulatory action before an event occurs.
The warning also arrives amid wider UK government efforts to strengthen cyber resilience across both public and private sectors. Previous guidance from the NCSC has addressed supply chain risks, cloud security and state-sponsored threats. This latest assessment extends that work into the realm of AI-enabled attacks, signaling that policymakers view the technology as a near-term operational risk rather than a distant hypothetical.
No specific attack, target, or timeline beyond 2028 was detailed in the available reporting. The NCSC's statement reflects a risk assessment rather than evidence of an imminent or planned attack.
Market Impact
For now, the warning is a policy and security signal rather than a market-moving event. It may accelerate spending on cybersecurity firms, AI-driven threat detection tools, and infrastructure resilience projects as UK organizations respond to the guidance.
Insurers covering cyber risk and operators of critical infrastructure are likely to review their defenses given the NCSC's assessment. Any concrete policy or regulatory response stemming from this warning was not detailed in current reporting.
The NCSC's warning underscores growing concern that AI is reshaping cyber threats facing essential services. How the UK government and infrastructure operators respond in the coming years will shape the country's resilience against this evolving risk.
Frequently Asked Questions
What exactly did the NCSC warn about?
The National Cyber Security Centre said an AI-powered ransomware attack on UK critical national infrastructure is highly likely by 2028.
Which sectors are considered at risk?
Reports point to critical national infrastructure broadly, which typically includes energy, water, transport and healthcare systems.
Has a specific attack already been detected?
No. The warning is a forward-looking risk assessment, not confirmation of a planned or ongoing attack.
Why is AI seen as increasing ransomware risk?
AI tools can automate reconnaissance, improve phishing content, and speed up identification of software vulnerabilities, making attacks faster and more accessible to attackers.

Britain’s top cyber defense agency has put a date on a scenario security teams have been dreading. The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says it is “highly likely” that AI-powered malware will feature in a ransomware attack on the UK’s critical national infrastructure between now and 2028.
The forecast arrived on November 3, 2026, alongside the NCSC’s annual review, titled “State of the Cyber Nation.” The agency also released a separate assessment examining how AI could reshape the cyber threat landscape over the next two years.
What the NCSC actually said
Dr. Richard Horne, CEO of the NCSC, indicated that AI is not producing entirely new methods of attack. Instead, it is amplifying familiar weaknesses, with social engineering and ransomware at the top of the list.
The assessment connects this shift to decades of underinvestment in cybersecurity technology. In other words, AI is exploiting gaps that were already there, not carving out fresh ones.
The NCSC did not spell out what form the AI-driven malware might take. It did, however, flag a potential increase in both the scale and efficiency of attacks carried out by state-backed groups and criminal gangs alike.
China named as the top threat
The reports single out hostile states, with China identified as the most significant threat.

articles.summary: ‘Highly likely’ AI will be used in ransomware attack on UK critical infrastructure  New Civil Engineer
articles.full_text:
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has warned that it is “highly likely AI malware will be used in a ransomware attack on UK critical national infrastructure (CNI)” and the head of the centre said it could happen within two years.
The warning was shared in the NCSC’s annual State of the Cyber Nation report, which was published today (3 November).
In last week’s Budget, the government announced £70M for a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (Nerv) Centre, which will be part of the NCSC.
Nerv will “identify vulnerabilities across critical infrastructure”, according to the NCSC.
In its report published today, the NCSC said: “The cyber threat to the UK’s CNI remains enduring. The NCSC continued to observe activity affecting CNI and its supporting ecosystem, including activity believed to be linked to nation states.
“Such activity may be intended to gather intelligence, gain access to sensitive networks, or establish a foothold in systems of strategic interest.”
It went on to single out threats posed by Russia and China.
“Russian hacking groups engage in offensive cyber operations in Ukraine, including disrupting power generation,” it said.
“Critical infrastructure and government institutions continue to be targeted by state actors, including a massive breach of government personnel records.”
In August, it was reported that hackers linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) were understood to have successfully shut down a “small” UK power station.
The NCSC report added: “China highly likely has the intent and is best positioned to use AI for operations against critical national infrastructure and other strategic targets.”
“The development of its own frontier AI capability programmes will almost certainly allow China to improve the identification of vulnerabilities, increase targeting efficiency and enhance access operations against critical national infrastructure and other strategic targets.”
At an event about today’s report, National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) CEO Richard Horne is expected to say: “In the coming months, we face a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents.
“But we must be clear that is not because AI has invented new ways to attack us. But because vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long can now be discovered and exploited at a scale that was once unimaginable.”
He said: “For decades, we have collectively got away with doing tech on the cheap.”
Horne continued: “We can be a nation where leaders of all organisations actively choose to invest with urgency. And where all organisations make security and resilience a fundamental requirement, not an afterthought.”
The warnings from the NCSC come as fridges and freezers in continental European supermarkets were deliberately switched to overheat and ruin food in a cyberattack this week.

articles.summary: The NCSC says AI-powered cyber attacks are coming for UK firms – but they still need to sharpen up on basic security practices  IT Pro
articles.full_text:
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has warned UK infrastructure is likely to fall victim to repeated AI-powered cyber attacks in the next two years, probably from Russia, China, and other hostile nation states.
The agency's latest State of the Cyber Nation report claims the use of AI within critical national infrastructure has left military networks, airports, hospitals, power stations, and businesses with an increased attack surface for adversaries to exploit.
"In the coming months, we face a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents," said NCSC CEO Richard Horne.
"But we must be clear that is not because AI has invented new ways to attack us, but because vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long can now be discovered and exploited at a scale that was once unimaginable."
The NCSC specifically highlighted growing threats posed by ransomware, social engineering, and vulnerability exploitation – all of which are areas the agency can offer support with.
Indeed, the NCSC said organizations across the UK should make better use of the tools, standards, and frameworks that already exist and have been shown to work against both conventional and AI-powered cyber attacks.
Cyber Essentials should be the starting point for cybersecurity, not the end goal, he said, with organizations building greater resilience according to their size, complexity, and risk.

A large part of the problem is that organizations are simply not spending enough, according to Horne.

“We can be a nation where leaders of all organizations actively choose to invest with urgency, and where all organizations make security and resilience a fundamental requirement, not an afterthought. The collective result would be a source of enduring national strength for us all."
State-sponsored threats are rising
State-sponsored actors such as China and Russia, for example, are highly likely to remain the greatest threat, according to the NCSC. China, while its home-grown chips lag behind in quality, has made significant strides in AI capabilities.
Observation also shows Russian cyber actors have been taking advantage of open source AI models, with hackers adapting and retraining them to suit their intelligence requirement needs, rather than developing in-house capabilities from scratch.
"We need every organization in the UK to take action now. Not only to protect their customers, services and livelihoods, but because cyber security is now part of the frontline defence of our nation," said Anne Keast-Butler, director of GCHQ.
"That means modernising technology and building resilience at the pace demanded by a rapidly changing world. It means moving from understanding cyber risk to reducing it. And it means preparing for disruption, ensuring essential services can be maintained, recovery can happen quickly, and organizations can operate with confidence during periods of heightened threat."
NCSC hails increased investment
The government has been doing its bit to help, according to the NCSC. In recent months, Downing Street has announced a series of investments aimed at bolstering cyber resilience across the country.
This includes £60 million to develop the first phase of a national Cyber Shield, £70 million for a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre to identify vulnerabilities across critical infrastructure and the economy.
Elsewhere, a new AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence in Manchester will help develop world-leading AI security expertise within government.
Trevor Dearing, senior director of critical infrastructure at Illumio, said the NCSC paints a concerning picture of the scale of threats facing UK organizations.
“Recent attacks on water systems, telecoms and even supermarket refrigeration shouldn’t be seen as isolated incidents. Each shows attackers where systems are weak and how operators respond, which a patient adversary could use to plan something far harder to recover from," he commented.
Dearing added that given most attacks still rely on stolen credentials and lateral movement, the NCSC is "right to get organizations to focus on fixing the basics".
"All organizations, not just CNI operators, need to strengthen the human layer against AI-enhanced social engineering, close off unnecessary internet exposure, and invest in detecting and containing lateral movement," he said.

articles.full_text:
The United Kingdom is facing an increasingly complex cybersecurity threat, with hostile state-sponsored groups and sophisticated cybercriminals potentially targeting critical national infrastructure. The growing use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in cyber operations is adding another dimension to the threat landscape, raising concerns about the ability of attackers to launch more advanced, automated, and difficult-to-detect cyberattacks. Critical sectors such as defense, energy, transportation, and emergency services are particularly vulnerable to these emerging risks.
One of the major concerns is the growing number of cyberattacks targeting Internet of Things (IoT) devices connected to networks across the world, particularly in Europe. As smart devices become increasingly integrated into everyday operations, they also create additional entry points for cybercriminals. Devices such as smart refrigerators, remotely operated freezers, industrial sensors, and other internet-connected equipment can become potential targets when security controls are inadequate.
Recent cyber incidents have highlighted how even seemingly ordinary connected devices can be exploited to disrupt essential operations. Reports of attacks involving remotely accessible refrigeration systems have raised concerns about the security of IoT infrastructure. Such threats are not limited to European countries such as France but have also extended to organizations and facilities in the United States.
Reports of disruptions involving refrigeration equipment at US military facilities have further highlighted the potential security implications of compromised connected devices, with suspicions raised about possible involvement by state-backed hacking groups.
These developments demonstrate that cyber threats are no longer confined to traditional computer networks, government databases, or financial institutions. Increasingly, attackers are exploring vulnerabilities in connected equipment and operational technology that support essential services. A successful compromise of such systems could potentially affect supply chains, military operations, food storage facilities, and other critical functions.
Highlighting these growing concerns, Richard Horne, Chief Executive of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), warned that the country must prepare for a new generation of AI-powered cyberattacks. He indicated that the coming two years could bring significant challenges as malicious actors increasingly use AI to improve the speed, scale, and sophistication of their cyber operations. Defense, energy, transportation, and emergency supply networks are among the sectors that require particular attention.
In the NCSC’s annual State of Cyber Security report, Horne emphasized the importance of strengthening Britain’s cyber resilience and improving its ability to identify, prevent, and respond to emerging threats. The growing accessibility of AI technologies could enable attackers to automate certain malicious activities, identify system vulnerabilities more efficiently, and develop convincing phishing campaigns targeting individuals and organizations.
Against this backdrop, the UK must prioritize investment in advanced cybersecurity technologies, strengthen public-private partnerships, and improve the protection of critical infrastructure. Organizations should also regularly assess their security frameworks, update vulnerable systems, and ensure that connected devices are protected through robust authentication and continuous monitoring.
Ultimately, cybersecurity must become a national priority rather than simply an IT responsibility. Building a resilient digital infrastructure will require coordinated efforts from government agencies, private organizations, technology providers, and the public. As AI continues to reshape the cyber threat landscape, Britain’s ability to strengthen its defenses today will play a crucial role in safeguarding its national security and maintaining public confidence in essential services over the coming decade.

articles.summary: 8,800-ton warship concept unveiled, packs over 100 missiles and 100 kW laser  Interesting EngineeringNaval Group unveils new drone carrier concept  Breaking DefenseNAVAL GROUP UNVEILS ITS NEW CONCEPT SHIP DESIGNED FOR NAVAL WARFARE OF THE FUTURE  Naval GroupTwo Superstructures, Railgun, and Drones: Naval Group Unveils the SCX 26  МілітарнийFrance Unveils Ambitious SCX26 Stealth Destroyer Program as European Combat Ships Fall Further Behind  Milit...
articles.full_text:
French shipbuilder Naval Group has unveiled a warship concept that combines a large missile arsenal with drone operations, an electromagnetic gun and a high-energy laser. The 170-meter SCX 26 concept illustrates how next-generation surface combatants could operate in naval warfare.
Presented at the Euronaval 2026 defense exhibition in Paris, the concept displaces approximately 8,818 US tons (8,000 tonnes) and is designed to reach 30 knots, with a range exceeding 8,000 nautical miles. Its proposed weapons fit includes more than 100 vertical launch system (VLS) cells, a rapid-fire electromagnetic gun, and a 100-kilowatt laser.
The SCX 26 is a design study and not a ship currently scheduled for construction. Naval Group describes it as an exercise in exploring technologies and architectures that could shape future naval warfare.
A warship designed around drones
One of the concept’s most prominent features is a large mission bay at the stern, designed to support the deployment, recovery, and maintenance of uncrewed systems. Integrated lifting equipment and a large-capacity elevator would allow the ship to handle different types of drones and helicopters.
The bay could be reconfigured depending on the mission, accommodating systems for intelligence gathering, surveillance, electronic warfare, anti-submarine warfare, and force protection. This would allow the vessel to operate as more than a conventional missile-armed combatant. It could also coordinate a wider network of crewed ships, aircraft and uncrewed platforms operating across the air, surface and underwater environments.
The ship’s architecture is divided into two integrated modules separated by a flexible zone. This arrangement is intended to make it easier to introduce new capabilities as technologies and operational requirements change, rather than requiring major redesigns throughout the vessel’s service life.
More than 100 missile cells and a 100 kW laser
The SCX 26’s proposed armament combines weapons intended for different engagement ranges and threats. Its main missile battery comprises more than 100 VLS cells of different classes, distributed between the bow and stern.
Vertical launch systems allow missiles to be stored and fired directly from cells built into a ship’s deck. Depending on the launcher and missile combination, they can accommodate weapons for air defense, anti-submarine warfare, and land or surface attack.
For closer-range defense, the ship would carry two Rampart modular launching systems and a 100 kW laser. High-energy lasers concentrate electrical energy into a beam that can heat and damage a target. They could provide another option against drones and other relatively inexpensive threats without requiring a conventional missile for every engagement. The effectiveness depends on factors such as weather, atmospheric conditions, range, and the ability to maintain the beam on a target.
The electromagnetic gun is another proposed feature. Unlike conventional naval guns that use chemical propellants, electromagnetic guns use electrical energy to accelerate projectiles. The concept specifies a rapid-fire capability but does not provide details about the weapon’s caliber, range, or performance.
Sensors and survivability built into the design
The concept also includes a UHF radar intended for ballistic missile defense, a comprehensive sonar suite for detecting underwater threats, and advanced electronic warfare systems. These would give the vessel a broad view of activity around it, from incoming aerial threats to submarines and electronic interference.
Naval Group has also emphasized redundancy and segregation in the ship’s design. Its two masts and the distribution of launchers between the bow and stern are intended to reduce dependence on individual systems or locations.
The proposed crew consists of 150 sailors, with accommodation for another 100 personnel, including commanders and specialists. Automation and artificial intelligence would help operators assess information and coordinate systems, while humans would remain responsible for operational decisions.

US Vice President JD Vance has blamed the war on Iran for his party’s withering midterms defeat, suggesting that the conflict may not have been worth ceding control of the United States Congress to Democrats.
“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote in a lengthy post on X. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so.”
Recommended Stories
“Everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”
Mark Pfeifle, who served as deputy national security adviser under President George W Bush, told Al Jazeera that Vance was owning up to a political failure of the administration’s own making.
“If you mess up, fess up!” he said, saying Vance was speaking up to convey that “my name was on the ballot two years ago. I have to take responsibility for this”, in a sign of political maturity and readiness to tackle Republicans’ biggest political liabilities.
MAGA heir
Vance, a likely 2028 presidential candidate and heir apparent to US President Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement, has been a key negotiator as the US and Iran search for a way out of the eight-month conflict, which has dented their economies and pushed global fuel prices up.
His statements on Tehran have been more dovish than those of other key members of the administration, and his post-election note appears to mark the closest he has yet come to publicly diverging from Trump on an issue that looks set to dog Republicans as the war continues.
“Vance is definitely trying to distance himself from Trump, as many other respectable Republicans will do over the next several weeks and months,” said Nick Rahall, a former Democratic member of Congress. “The people have spoken.”
“It had even leaked before that JD was the only one in Trump’s inner circle who had questions and was hesitant about Iran [war] from the beginning,” Rahall added.
Citing a pollster he describes as “one of the smartest people I know”, Vance said he was told ending the Iran war and “changing our relationship with Israel” were two of the top four answers given by Americans surveyed who had voted for Trump in 2024 but were planning to vote for Democrats in the 2026 midterms.
In stark contrast, Trump said, in the wake of the rebuke at the ballot box, that he had no regrets about launching the conflict.
“I did the right thing. I would have done it again,” he told the Wall Street Journal.

articles.title: Iran's political, religious leaders shift stance to support nuclear weapons as war looms - report - The Jerusalem Post
articles.summary: Iran's political, religious leaders shift stance to support nuclear weapons as war looms - report  The Jerusalem Post
articles.full_text:
An increasing number of Iranian clerics and officials are pressing Iranian leaders to reverse their pledge not to pursue nuclear weapons, the New York Times reported on Wednesday.
In past decades, Iranian officials have publicly endorsed the fatwa issued by supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei forbidding the development and use of nuclear weapons.
However, US and Israeli intelligence agencies have reported signs that Iran was enriching uranium to levels close to those needed for a nuclear weapon.
The NYT cited regional analysts as saying Khamenei had hoped to keep Iran's nuclear intentions ambiguous in hopes of deterring attacks on Iran without needing to actually develop a nuclear weapon.
Instead, Israel and the US started the 12-day war in 2025, and then another war in 2026, and Iranians have grown increasingly in favor of having a nuclear weapon as a result.
“He created this neither in nor out situation, where they paid for a bomb they didn’t have,” Mohammad Ali Shabani, an Iran analyst who edits the independent regional news site Amwaj.media, told the NYT.
“Now, there is this sense that unless you have this ultimate weapon, you could end up at the mercy of not just the US, but Israel, at any point.”
Politicians call for withdrawal from NPT
Politicians have begun calling for Iran to withdraw from the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT). On Saturday, Iranian Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei said that Iran's leaders were discussing the nuclear debate.
“No new decision has been made yet,” he said. “Of course, the debate now is whether we want to keep the same doctrine we had before the war, if war breaks out again.”
While advocating for withdrawing from the NPT was once a minority opinion, Mohammad Ghaderi, a foreign affairs expert in Tehran, told the NYT that it has become a majority view.
In addition to the politicians, many religious leaders are also preaching the necessity of nuclear power, despite the late Ayatollah's fatwa.
“The taboo is gone,” Shabani told the NYT. “A religious foundation for the shift is here. The question is whether a strategic or political shift will follow.”
Pezeshkian, Rouhani, back peaceful nuclear doctrine
Some Iranian leaders, including President Masoud Pezeshkian and former president Hassan Rouhani, still back the idea of a peaceful nuclear doctrine, according to the NYT.
Former Iranian diplomat Kourosh Ahmadi warned in Iran's leading reformist newspaper, Shargh, that the pro-nuclear weapon rhetoric coming from prominent leaders "is dangerous because it makes the work of officials trying to prevent another war more difficult.”
Additionally, Ahmadi said, the chances of being attacked while building the bomb would be increased.
However, it is getting increasingly harder for critics of nuclear weapons to justify their position, Sina Toossi, an Iran expert at the Center for International Policy, a Washington-based think tank, told the NYT.
“The central problem for advocates of restraint is explaining what Iran gained from remaining below the nuclear threshold,” he said, adding that a new round of US strikes “could strengthen the very arguments for the nuclear weapons that Washington says it wants to prevent.”

articles.title: Bukele’s warning to Haitian gang leaders that his forces will 'finish' them as he did in El Salvador - Fox News
articles.summary: Bukele’s warning to Haitian gang leaders that his forces will 'finish' them as he did in El Salvador  Fox NewsEl Salvador’s President Takes a High-Stakes Gamble Confronting Haitian Gangs  WSJEl Salvador’s Bukele touts military intervention in Haiti  Al JazeeraHaiti’s prime minister Fils-Aimé speaks out as concerns over El Salvador’s troops deepen  AP NewsBukele's gang offensive goes abroad as El Salvador rushes troops to Haiti  Reuters
articles.full_text:
After crushing powerful criminal gangs in El Salvador, President Nayib Bukele has turned his attention to the Caribbean nation of Haiti, deploying 2,000 troops after four Salvadoran military aviation technicians disappeared following an Oct.18 ambush near Port-au-Prince.
"We have already finished with the gangs in El Salvador, and we can finish with you too," Bukele wrote in a message on X directed at Haiti's criminal groups. Bukele stressed that the operation's objective was not to invade Haiti or conduct a long-term occupation, but to recover the four missing Salvadorans alive.
The disappearance has become a national priority for Bukele, who has warned Haitian gang leaders that El Salvador is prepared to use overwhelming force if the men are not returned alive.
The aviation technicians were assigned to a medical unit as part of the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) in Haiti when their armored vehicle was attacked in Croix-des-Bouquets. Haiti’s National Police announced Tuesday, more than two weeks after the attack, that it had found the charred remains of the vehicle in the Santo neighborhood of Croix-des-Bouquets. Police said, however, they found no sign of the missing men.
El Salvador says the men were abducted, the Haitian government says the soldiers are missing, and one gang leader says they are dead.
In a post on X Tuesday, directed at the "Haitian people" and written in Haitian creole, Bukele recalled the 1806 assassination of Jean-Jacques Dessalines, who proclaimed Haiti’s independence from France in 1804 and who many regard as the founder of Haiti.
"Dessalines liberated Haiti, but some people who were by his side betrayed him and killed him," Bukele said. "Those traitors still exist in Haiti."
Bukele also reposted video of a helicopter engagement in Croix-des-Bouquets.
"Gangs were attacking GSF soldiers from Chad," he wrote. "We arrived quickly and repelled the attackers with our attack helicopters."
Bukele has the backing of President Donald Trump, who, when asked by reporters at Mar-a-Lago on Halloween, confirmed speaking with the Salvadoran president.
"He said that he has a big problem with Haiti," Trump said. "They killed some of his people. I said, 'You're running your country. You have to do what you have to do.'"
Unlike previous foreign interventions, Bukele's deployment has the backing of Haiti's transitional government.
"The international force is not here to replace the state," Haitian Prime Minister Didier Fils-Aimé said Tuesday in his first remarks about the deployment. "They're here to support us."
Fils-Aimé added that Bukele "understands our fight. … He came to stand on the side of the Haitian people."
The operation has drawn criticism from human-rights advocates and gang leaders who warn that a military escalation could worsen civilian suffering. The U.N. says at least 5,700 people have been killed or injured due to the gang violence in Haiti since Jan. 1 as security forces struggle to contain the violence.
The U.N. has also indicated that El Salvador’s deployment is separate from the GSF and has warned El Salvador must follow applicable international law.
One of those gang leaders is Wilson Joseph, known as "Lanmò Sanjou," leader of the powerful 400 Mawozo gang. He accused rival gang Chen Mechan of carrying out the ambush and claimed the Salvadorans are dead, he told The Associated Press.
Joseph also sent a letter to United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres asking the U.N. for mediation and warning Bukele's "vengeful remarks, expectations, and threats … will lead to an escalation of violence and a logic of reprisals, of which the Haitian people would be the first victims."
Joseph was indicted by the U.S. in 2022 on hostage-taking charges related to the 2021 kidnapping of 17 missionaries, including 16 Americans, and remains the subject of a reward of up to $1 million for his arrest.
Bukele dismissed such appeals, accusing gang leaders of attempting to use civilians and international concerns about human rights as a shield to preserve their power and avoid accountability. Bukele has said that negotiations have only prolonged the crisis that has devastated Haiti for years.
After years as one of the world's most violent countries, dominated by powerful gangs including MS-13, El Salvador launched an unprecedented crackdown in 2022 under a state of emergency. Authorities carried out tens of thousands of arrests, ultimately detaining more than 90,000 suspected gang members.
Supporters credit the strategy with driving homicide rates to historic lows and restoring public safety. Critics accuse Bukele's government of human-rights abuses, arbitrary detentions and erosion of due-process protections.
The question now is whether that model can be exported to Haiti, where gangs control large portions of Port-au-Prince and wield influence over key transportation routes and neighborhoods. Despite years of international intervention, security conditions have continued to deteriorate.
The GSF has struggled with manpower shortages and operational limitations, operating below its Security Council-approved intended strength, leaving Haiti's government unable to reassert full control over much of the capital.
"We can help you defeat them, but we are not your enemies," Bukele wrote on Tuesday. "We must stand up, take back control of our communities, and put under our control those who are making us endure all this pain, all this suffering. We are right there beside you… Haiti will be free."
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Can Democrats stop Iran war, reverse Trump’s tariffs after midterms win? - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Can Democrats stop Iran war, reverse Trump’s tariffs after midterms win?  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
Democrats have taken control of the United States House of Representatives and Senate in Tuesday’s midterm elections in a scathing defeat for US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party.
The Congress that will convene in early January will be radically different from the first two years of Trump’s second presidential term, which saw Republicans holding majorities in both chambers.
While Democrats will have greater power to scrutinise Trump’s policies and obstruct any legislation they oppose, there is still a lot a president can do without congressional approval.
Here is a look at some pressing political issues and how a Democratic majority in both chambers might affect them:
The US-Israel war on Iran
Trump has acknowledged the role the war on Iran has played in Republican losses in the midterm elections. “I think a part of it was Iran, but at the same time, people understood the importance of what I’ve done with Iran,” Trump said during a telephone interview with Fox News.
Frustration among voters about inflation, and the rising cost of fuel and groceries have been among the main factors behind their rebuke to Republicans. Democrats tapped into this by campaigning heavily on affordability and domestic spending.
Trump embarked on the war on Iran with Israel in February without congressional authorisation. He could still order attacks, but he could also face constraints from the new Congress. Lawmakers could use their power to deny additional funding when the current government-funding bill expires on December 11, presenting a critical budget constraint on Trump’s military decisions.
However, James Boys, research fellow at the Centre on US Politics at University College London, said that while Congress may wish to cut off funding, it may not be straightforward. “With troops in theatre, this would prove to be highly problematic and be seen to be placing American lives at risk,” he said.
Analysts also said the War Powers Resolution is unlikely to succeed in reining Trump in. Previous attempts to use the 1973 federal law have been defeated or rendered ineffective.
The War Powers Resolution states that a president can repel an imminent attack, but military actions must end within 60 days unless Congress declares war. The president can then issue a veto, which can only be overcome by a two-thirds supermajority in both the House and Senate.
The projected breakdown of the newly elected Congress shows that Democrats are well short of those supermajority thresholds.
Scott Lucas, professor of international politics at the UCD Clinton Institute in Dublin, Ireland, said that while Congress is constrained without a two-thirds majority, what it could do is propose legislation by “working with some Republicans who might distance themselves from Trump” after the resounding declaration of dissatisfaction voters have given the president in these midterm elections.
For example, he said, “JD Vance, the vice president, opposed the war and has done so from the start.” Last week, Vance sent a letter to Iran’s security chief in a reported effort to revive talks and avert further attacks.
“[Will] he now push even harder to end the war?” Lucas asked.
However, Boys said the fact that Trump no longer faces election himself because the US Constitution requires him to leave office at the end of his second term may make the president instead feel that “he is now unleashed to act with impunity on the world stage”.
“Indeed, given his weakened domestic political circumstances, one can easily imagine Donald Trump escalating policies in the Middle East as he seeks to establish an indisputable presidential legacy,” he added.
Tariffs and international trade
Last year, Trump unleashed tariffs of 10 percent to 50 percent on about 90 countries with the aim of shrinking the US trade deficit. The move, which rattled global markets, was struck down by the Supreme Court in February, but the Trump administration has found workarounds to that ruling.
Days after the Supreme Court’s 6-3 vote, Trump doubled down on the tariffs, quickly signing an executive order based on a different statute and raising them from 10 percent to 15 percent. However, those tariffs are limited to 150 days unless they are extended by Congress.
Democrats have blamed Trump’s tariffs for exacerbating the rising cost-of-living crisis as tariffs ultimately fall back on US importers who pass them on to consumers. They accused Trump of “pickpocketing the American people”. A Democratic-controlled Congress could push for exceptions that would give exporters some temporary relief, but any deeper shift in US trade policy will have to wait for the 2028 presidential election and the new occupant of the White House.
Boys said the “situation regarding tariffs remains before the United States courts” and whether the government must give back tariff money it has already collected – and exactly how much of it – remains in dispute.
The one area in which Congress is expected to follow through regardless of the flip in party control is in passing tougher restrictions on China’s access to technology. These include the Remote Access Security Act, which would extend export controls to remote access of US goods, software or technology, and the Chip Security Act, which would require companies to verify that advanced artificial intelligence chips remain in authorised locations to prevent diversion to foreign adversaries.
Immigration and border control
Lucas said one major outcome of the midterm vote is that Democrats will now assume the chairmanships of all congressional committees, which have the power to launch investigations and subpoena witnesses.
This could result in scrutiny of the Trump family’s vast business empire, the president’s ties with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s handling of the war with Iran. They could even try to impeach Trump for a third time over the conflict.
Congress also may – and plans to – launch extensive investigations into the Trump administration’s immigration policies. Democrats have repeatedly advocated for using their new subpoena power to scrutinise collaboration between the US tax agency, the Internal Revenue Service, and the Department of Homeland Security on the Trump administration’s policy of deporting refugees and migrants.
Detaining people at airports and hearings in their immigration cases became part of Trump’s efforts to carry out mass deportations – one of his 2024 campaign promises. In the lead-up to Tuesday’s elections, Fox News released a poll that found 53 percent of registered voters felt the immigration crackdown had “gone too far”.
The Homeland Security Department has argued that about 70 percent of its immigration detainees are criminals, if pending charges are factored in. But critics have questioned that statistic, given that the legal system in the US gives suspects the presumption of innocence until they are proven guilty in a court of law.
Lucas said the midterm vote means “Democrats and responsible Republicans can now reach out to the state and local communities and encourage them to pursue recovery and responsible policies.”

articles.title: NCSC Annual Review 2026 warns AI-powered malware could target UK critical infrastructure by 2028 - Industrial Cyber
articles.summary: NCSC Annual Review 2026 warns AI-powered malware could target UK critical infrastructure by 2028  Industrial Cyber
articles.full_text:
The U.K.’s critical national infrastructure should prepare for ransomware attacks involving artificial intelligence-powered malware by 2028, according to a warning from the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), part of the signals intelligence agency GCHQ. In its State of the Cyber Nation report, published Nov. 3, the NCSC said it is highly likely that hostile actors will increase their use of AI over the next two years to expand the scale and efficiency of cyber operations, including ransomware attacks, social engineering and vulnerability exploitation.
In its ‘NCSC Annual Review 2026’, the agency warned that AI could enable attackers to identify and exploit longstanding cybersecurity weaknesses at unprecedented speed and scale. Highlighting that AI does not necessarily introduce new attack methods but increases the speed and scale at which existing vulnerabilities can be discovered and exploited, the agency urged organizations to improve foundational cybersecurity investments, reduce unnecessary internet connectivity and use Cyber Essentials as a starting point rather than an endpoint, while building resilience according to their size, complexity and risk.
“In the coming months, we face a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents. But we must be clear that is not because AI has invented new ways to attack us,” Richard Horne, NCSC CEO, said in a Tuesday statement. “But because vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long can now be discovered and exploited at a scale that was once unimaginable.”
He added, “For decades, we have collectively got away with doing tech on the cheap. We can be a nation where leaders of all organisations actively choose to invest with urgency… And where all organisations make security and resilience a fundamental requirement, not an afterthought. The collective result would be a source of enduring national strength for us all.”
Horne encourages U.K. organizations to ‘take the responsibility now to make different choices,’ including addressing the failure to adequately invest in their technology; not having technology unnecessarily connected to the internet; and making Cyber Essentials the starting point for cyber security, not the end goal, with organizations building greater resilience according to their size, complexity and risk.
He will say that failing to make these choices will result in leaders “having to look their investors, shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, in the eye and explain…when food isn’t on shelves, lights aren’t on, businesses have gone under.”
“The NCSC’s latest annual report shows cyber threats are growing more sophisticated,” Dan Jarvis, U.K.’s Minister of State for Security, said. “We’re using the power of AI to help stay ahead of those who seek to do us harm, with a new national Cyber Shield and an AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence.”
“New technologies are creating extraordinary opportunities for growth, innovation and prosperity. But they are also reshaping the cyber threat landscape,” Anne Keast-Butler, director of the GCHQ, said in the NCSC Annual Review 2026. “Artificial intelligence is accelerating change, increasing the scale and speed at which cyber threats can emerge, and exposing weaknesses in the technologies and systems we rely upon every day.”
She added that “across GCHQ and the NCSC, we are developing new approaches to cyber defence, including pioneering work on Cyber Shield and the responsible application of AI to strengthen the U.K.’s cyber resilience. But technology alone will not solve this challenge. We need every organisation in the U.K. to take action now. Not only to protect their customers, services and livelihoods, but because cyber security is now part of the frontline defence of our nation.”
The NCSC Annual Review 2026 said that Russian hacking groups engage in offensive cyber operations in Ukraine, including disrupting power generation. Critical infrastructure and government institutions continue to be targeted by state actors, including a massive breach of government personnel records. Meanwhile, U.K. telecoms and health sectors are victims of high-profile ransomware attacks in pursuit of financial gain.
The report identified “continuity in the actors we face and the tools they use. The most serious adversaries we face today are the same as they were a decade ago. Their core tactics have evolved, but their success still relies extensively on the targeted exploitation of the scaled and known vulnerabilities across government, economy and society. The bulk of capability we have seen deployed in recent state-backed incidents is not an advanced, autonomous end-to-end AI attack, but a much simpler exploitation of common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVEs) and other open vulnerabilities, based on a decade of operational experience, patience and understanding of what works.”
It noted that for large organisations, 88% of incidents came from four initial access vectors, including exploiting external public-facing applications, phishing, misuse of valid accounts, and exploiting external remote services.
“Organisations that modernise their technologies, address vulnerabilities and strengthen resilience are becoming more secure. Those that do not are finding it harder to keep pace with an evolving threat, as evidenced by recent attacks on programmable logic controllers (PLCs),” the NCSC said. “These attacks come at a time when the number of adversaries, state and non-state, continue to grow. Driving all of these developments is a world that’s far more confrontational than in 2015, in which cyber capabilities are now an increasingly important component of national power.”
The NCSC describes a more contested, competitive and technologically accelerated cyber environment, in which cyber attacks are increasingly used to shape economic outcomes, project state power and pursue strategic advantage. It identifies four interconnected trends.
The first is that China is changing the scale of cyber competition. Its activity is the most sophisticated and sustained challenge facing the U.K., driven by a ‘whole-of-state’ approach that combines legislation, private contractors and technology development. Data is central to this approach, since China uses its cyber capabilities to acquire vast amounts of information to train models, improve capability and generate insight. In December 2025, the U.K. sanctioned two China-based companies, i-Soon and Integrity Technology Group, for reckless and indiscriminate malicious cyber activity. In April 2026, the NCSC and 15 international partners issued a joint advisory on tactics believed to be used by most China-linked actors to disguise their activity.
The second trend is that cyber operations have become a tool of state power, used alongside diplomacy, economic pressure, military power and information operations. The growth of the commercial cyber intrusion marketplace has almost certainly lowered the barrier to entry, letting a broader range of actors conduct sophisticated operations. During periods of heightened tension, the threat can escalate rapidly and without warning. Russia currently represents the most audacious threat, while Iran-linked groups continue to cause indiscriminate disruption at scale.
In July 2026, the NCSC and 18 partners from 12 countries warned that FSB Centre 16 actors were exploiting vulnerable routers to target critical national infrastructure worldwide. The U.K. also sanctioned 24 individuals and entities behind destructive cyber and hybrid operations, and, with EU member states, attributed a December 2025 attack on Poland’s energy grid to the same FSB unit. Had it succeeded, it could have cut electricity to 500,000 citizens.
The third trend is that economic security depends on cyber security. Ransomware, data breaches and supply chain compromises disrupt operations, halt production and impose heavy recovery costs, and malicious cyber activity costs U.K. organisations an estimated £14.7 billion a year. Cyber espionage is highly likely to be the most significant threat to long-term economic growth, as it erodes innovation and competitive advantage, with knowledge-intensive sectors increasingly targeted.
The 2025 attack on Jaguar Land Rover illustrates the damage: it severely disrupted global production and retail activity and hit suppliers across the automotive sector. JLR reported about £196 million in direct costs, and the incident contributed to U.K. GDP growing by only 0.1% in Q3 2025, below forecasts.
The fourth trend is that technology advances are changing and increasing the threat, with the pace of change now the key difference. AI, automation and greater computing power are already helping some threat actors find vulnerabilities, target victims and operate more efficiently. By 2028, it is highly likely that China, Russia and other nation states will routinely use AI cyber to achieve geopolitical goals, and that AI-powered malware will have been used in a ransomware attack on U.K. critical national infrastructure. Growing reliance on space-based technologies will also widen the threat surface over the next ten years.
In response, the NCSC argues that the U.K. need not choose between today’s threats and tomorrow’s: well-understood vulnerabilities remain the main route for attackers, while new technology speeds up and scales their exploitation, so resilience must be strengthened now while preparing for what comes next. It also highlights threats to democracy, noting that hostile states continue to target election candidates, officials and institutions, with persistent spear-phishing of high-risk individuals and growing attempts to compromise messaging apps.

Editor's Note: This article reflects the views of its author, a Ukrainian Member of Parliament. Given his unique position and perspective, we believe his views offer a valuable contribution to ongoing discussions about the conflict and merit consideration by our readers.
NATO has yet to fully recognize that the strategic paradigm of the Cold War is no longer sufficient for the security environment it now faces. The alliance cannot meet the demands of modern warfare while relying on legacy assumptions, force structures, and deterrence concepts designed for a fundamentally different era. Adapting to today’s global reality requires not simply modernizing existing capabilities, but rethinking the foundations of how NATO organizes, equips, and prepares for conflict.
Since 2022, NATO’s policy can be broadly divided into two eras: the “Biden era” and the “Trump era.” The Biden era was characterized by an attempt to “stop the bleeding.” Adherence to an increasingly elusive status quo was the primary objective, with Biden stating that the U.S. will support Ukraine “as long as it takes” to win the war. Support to Ukraine was provided through existing, often outdated weapons and training of Ukrainian military personnel. However, this support was provided without a fundamental reassessment of the changes unfolding on the Ukrainian battlefield.
Conversely, the later Trump presidency changed this premise by introducing a different logic: shifting a greater share of defense spending to European allies while preserving U.S. nuclear dominance and leaving the existing structure of defense spending largely intact. At first glance, this may appear to represent a step forward; in practice, however, it carries serious risks and limitations.
Although both the Biden and Trump eras pushed NATO to adapt to a rapidly changing security environment, neither fully addressed the deeper transformation required by modern warfare. Preserving the status quo through legacy capabilities, higher defense spending, and nuclear deterrence is no longer sufficient. NATO must move beyond modernization and fundamentally transform its force structure, procurement, doctrine, and approach to technological innovation in order to prepare not only for the wars of today, but for the battlefield of tomorrow.
The Trump Era Pillars and Their Efficacy
From the Ukrainian perspective, the Trump-era approach rests on two central premises, each of which deserves closer scrutiny:
First, events in recent years show that the existence of a nuclear umbrella does not prevent the outbreak and escalation of conventional warfare. Even when aimed directly at a member of the nuclear club, states use creative and modern methods to maintain conflict below the threshold of nuclear war. This includes when strikes occur on one’s own territory—such as in regions of Russia or at U.S. military bases in the Persian Gulf. These escalations have yet to serve as grounds for the use of nuclear weapons. Paradoxically, the very fact of possessing nuclear weapons psychologically weakens such a possessor, who becomes overreliant upon their nuclear deterrent at the detriment of their conventional force capability, prioritizing funding for maintaining the nuclear component over the development of conventional armed forces. A striking example of this is the relentless desire of Poland and the Baltic states to host a U.S. nuclear arsenal on their territory, despite the utility of such an arsenal in decreasing Russian aggression being doubtful, if not contradictory.
Second, there is a prevailing assumption that the problem among NATO countries in the defense sector lies exclusively in the level of funding. All recent discussions and disputes within NATO are based on this premise—who is contributing enough and who is falling short. It was precisely this issue that formed the basis of the most recent NATO summits in The Hague and Ankara, which focused on the increase in defense spending to 3.5–5% of GDP. This effectively perpetuates the status quo, replicating the old military infrastructure to address outdated challenges and requirements, and hinders the modernization of military technology. It creates the illusion that defense capabilities are growing, even though in reality they are struggling to maintain pace with battlefield innovations. As was the case with Germany’s Bismarck battleship in World War II, a vast amount of resources were spent on armaments that were not up to the challenge of the times.
This is precisely where major problems arise. Currently, defense spending in the European part of NATO stands at about 2.2% of GDP. In the U.S., it is about 3.01% of GDP. In other words, NATO countries still have a long way to go to reach the target figures. But defense spending and its proposed drastic increase does not happen in a vacuum. These decisions are accompanied by constant political crises and resignations, as was recently the case in London. Or consider the heated debate in the U.S. and the slim chances of passing a proposal to increase defense spending to 1.5 trillion U.S. dollars. This is happening for entirely understandable reasons, since an increase in defense spending must be financed either by cutting social spending or by increasing the budget deficit, which, in turn, will lead to a rise in the debt burden. Let’s also consider proposals to modernize the most costly component of defense: nuclear arsenals. With these challenges, the situation begins to look completely hopeless, leading to a political crisis among NATO countries with planned defense spending targets unachievable and, in fact, illusory.
Are We Asking the Right Questions?
We must ask ourselves: do NATO countries really need a staggering increase in defense spending? Let’s compare. Ukraine spends approximately $84.1 billion annually on defense amid the war. Moscow spends approximately $190 billion. And, as recently acknowledged at the G-7 summit, Ukraine has at least parity on the battlefield despite the significant difference in spending. Meanwhile, the European part of NATO spends about $550 billion annually on defense. This is without a war, without the SAFE (Security Action for Europe) program, and without Ukraine’s budget. In other words, NATO’s spending advantage is more than double. And this is despite the fact that Ukraine is fighting successfully with far less funding. The difference is more staggering in the current U.S.-Iran conflict. The U.S. defense budget stands at $961.6 billion. For Iran, its annual defense spending is estimated at only $7.4 billion (although unofficial estimates suggest spending could reach as much as $25 billion). China’s annual defense spending is estimated at approximately $300–350 billion. Of course, purchasing power varies from country to country, but even these figures demonstrate the significant advantage NATO countries currently hold. The bottom line is that it does not matter how much a country spends, but what you spend on. Either you're fighting an old-style war, or you're preparing for new challenges.
Moreover, NATO countries have an advantage in technology and innovation. Space, the seas, and the air remain firmly in the hands of the Western world. It is extremely difficult to surpass this foundation—provided, of course, that it is actually utilized and made to function effectively. Although China and Russia are eager to catch up—for example, by deploying their own alternative to the Starlink network—the U.S. was still the pioneer in the field of unmanned systems and drones. Consider the MQ-9A Reaper or RQ-4B Global Hawk drones. Or, in fact, the first kamikaze drones in Ukraine—the American Switchblade 300/600.
An Outdated Approach to a Very Modern World
So what’s wrong, then? Rather than spending or capabilities, the main problem is that the defense sector is developing within an outdated framework that took shape as early as the late 20th century. The introduction of innovations in the field of weapons is extremely piecemeal and far too gradual, and is largely limited to the modernization of existing systems already in service with the armed forces. In essence, this is modernization, not transformation.
At the same time, very few fundamentally new types of weapons have appeared over the past 20 years, with rare exceptions such as the MQ-9A Reaper. The dominant role on the battlefield has traditionally been assigned to manned aircraft, aircraft carrier strike groups, and heavy armored vehicles. This concept was entirely justified throughout the Cold War, as virtually everything was built around these systems: personnel training, tactics and strategy for conducting combat operations, maintenance systems, logistics, and the corresponding infrastructure.
However, events on the battlefields in Ukraine and in the waters of the Persian Gulf show that such weapons systems often become irrelevant to current tasks and modern challenges. This does not negate the need to fund and further develop missile systems and, accordingly, air defense systems. However, without the ability to directly project force onto enemy territory—without “boots on the ground”—such systems do not, in and of themselves, become a decisive factor. Achieving this capability without the widespread use of unmanned technologies on the battlefield is becoming increasingly difficult, and in some cases, practically impossible.
At the same time, the development of unmanned technologies is increasingly taking the form of a full-fledged “arms race,” in which fielding only a limited number of units equipped with unmanned systems no longer has a significant impact on the battlefield. A widespread transition to a new range of weapons, in turn, will require a restructuring of virtually the entire infrastructure of the armed forces.
