SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — North Korea launched multiple missiles toward the sea on Wednesday, South Korea’s military said, hours after Pyongyang said it saw no need to resume diplomacy with Washington in protest of accusations that North Korean hackers were behind the recent cryptocurrency heist at Binance.
Observers say North Korea was likely pressuring the U.S. to drop what it calls its hostility against the North and offer concessions if it wants to restore ties between U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected the launches of several missiles fired toward North Korea’s eastern waters. It said South Korean and U.S. authorities were analyzing details of the launches. It said South Korea maintains a readiness to repel any potential provocations by North Korea.
Earlier Wednesday, Kim’s sister, senior official Kim Yo Jong, again disputed an FBI announcement that North Korean hackers were responsible for the hack at Binance, calling it “an extension of Washington’s invariable hostile policy toward” Pyongyang.
“It is our clear stand that we have no need to sit face to face with such unreliable and hostile persons,” she said. “The choice for peace includes dialogue of course, but this is not surely equated with national interests for us.”
In a Tuesday statement, she described the FBI announcement as “a trite provocation.”
Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said Friday that hackers stole more than $6 billion in what appears to be the largest cryptocurrency heist on record. The FBI later said the theft was orchestrated by North Korean hackers, attributing the attack to a hacking group known as TraderTraitor, which was also behind a $1.5 billion hack of the Bybit exchange last year.
In recent months, North Korea has accelerated its weapons tests in a likely bid to increase its leverage in potential diplomacy with the U.S. after Trump expressed his eagerness to restore diplomacy with Kim Jong Un. The news of the latest launches came amid vote counting in the U.S. midterm elections.
Also Wednesday, North Korea’s state KCNA news agency released a photo showing parts of a warship under construction that would likely be its biggest naval vessel. KCNA said Kim Jong Un expressed satisfaction this week during a visit to the Nampho Shipyard over the warship that it said “is incomparably huge” relative to its 5,000-ton destroyers. Kim previously said North Korea planned to build a 10,000-ton strategic guided missile cruiser.
Tensions between the two Koreas have also deepened since mine blasts at their border in September wounded three South Korean soldiers. Seoul accused North Korea of burying the mines south of the border and demanded an apology. Pyongyang has denied responsibility for the explosions and warned of retaliation if provoked.
North Korea later threatened to resume propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts and place new weapons systems along the border.

articles.summary: Why tradwives are fleeing the movement: ‘I can’t undo my past – but I can warn other women’  The GuardianThe tradwives are revolting  The ObserverExploring the ‘Trad-Wife’ Phenomenon  CountercurrentsIs It Possible To Be A Feminist And A Tradwife?  Her Campus"It Absolutely Robbed Me Of My Personhood": 14 Tradwives Are Getting Really, Really Honest About What It's Actually Like, And I Think Every Young Woman Considering This Lifestyle Needs To Hear What They...

When Bernadine Bluntly posted a video earlier this year renouncing the tradwife movement she had championed, it caused shockwaves through the “alt-right” social media world. Previously, posts of her and her six children had flooded feeds as the Maga movement gained ground. She was one of the defiantly anti-feminist influencers who promoted a return to patriarchal gender roles, pronatalist ideals and fundamentalist Christian values – particularly around the sanctity of marriage. Bluntly, whose real surname is Barber, had, in the past, sold T-shirts reading “RIP Feminism”, supported Brett Kavanaugh’s nomination to the supreme court and developed a course, Simply Smitten, to help young women attract husbands who were “traditional masculine men”.
Then, last year, she left her husband. Her divorce was finalised this year. In the proceedings, she got a restraining order against her ex, whom she said was abusive (he denies this). In April, the 36-year-old posted a video titled: “What I got wrong about the trad movement”, in which she said that, while she is still a Christian and believes in the differences between men and women: “I no longer believe in extreme gender roles, especially when they’re wrapped in spiritual language and used to justify control, silence or harm.” She said that the tradwife movement, one she initially thought was about a “return to strong family values”, has “become indistinguishable from the current wave of the red-pill manosphere”. She concluded: “If my past content contributed to that, I am so genuinely sorry.”
Bluntly is part of a growing movement of ex-tradwife influencers. Even those who have not outrightly denounced the term seem to be distancing themselves from it. Nara Smith, the model and influencer who was married at 18, had four children by the time she was 24 and posts content of herself wearing cutesy dresses to cook for her husband to her 12.5m TikTok and 4.8m Instagram followers, told the Guardian last month that there is no secret tradwife “agenda” to her content. Even 36-year-old Hannah Neeleman, perhaps the archetypal modern tradwife, appeared to backpedal from the movement in a recent interview with New York magazine. Neeleman’s content, which she posts as Ballerina Farm, romanticises the homestead lifestyle of her Mormon family on their Utah ranch and became a blueprint for other tradwife wannabes. She and her husband have nine children, rear cattle and pigs and have built a 10m-strong following on Instagram. “If there’s things that I’m sharing that people think are actually doing harm to our sex, then OK, let me take the feedback,” she said.
Jennie Gage, 52, was one of the first ex-tradwife influencers. She grew up in what she describes as a “very traditional, old-fashioned” Mormon family in Arizona. Gage went to scripture evenings, studied Bible texts and, at 12, joined her church’s women’s programme, where she was taught how to care for children, iron men’s shirts and clean toilets. It was, she says, an “immersion programme to prepare you for tradwife life”.
At 18, Gage got engaged, but was told by a church bishop that God wanted her to be with another man, whom she ended up marrying six weeks later. From the outside, her 24 years of marriage seemed idyllic – raising five children, cooking and feeding chickens. She was a Maga devotee; her social media profile picture was of Donald Trump and she was elated when he was elected. But behind closed doors, she says, she was in an abusive marriage, in which she was forbidden from working or having a bank account. When she caught her husband meeting a sex worker in 2018, she left him, her church and her politics behind.
Some of her ex-tradwife content is mocking: in one TikTok, she posts a video recorded during her tradwife years, in which she shows off the cookies she had prepared for her ex, who was heading off on a long journey for work. “I view my role as, like, you know when you’re flying and the flight attendants get you all your stuff and everything?” she said to camera. That video now makes her “want to barf”, she writes in the description. But there is also the more serious problem of the financial ruin that trad women can be left with when they leave a breadwinning husband who has total control of the household budget. “I can’t go back and undo my past and erase all the horrible things I had to go through,” Gage tells me over a video call from her home in Arizona. But she can, she says, “warn other people” against the trad lifestyle – something she wishes someone had done for her.
“I’m not out to fight Ballerina Farm,” Gage says. “Because [Hannah Neeleman] is financially safe. I’m out to fight women not being financially safe.” For most of her marriage, Gage was given cash in an envelope to go grocery shopping. “If it wasn’t enough money, I would just put stuff back,” she says. After the couple divorced, Gage says she was left with nothing. She set up a GoFundMe to pay for her divorce lawyer and borrowed money from friends and family to survive. Now, she tells young women, by all means: “Have babies, get married, fall in love. But have a prenup, have a spousal trust, make sure that retirement’s in your name.”
Tia Levings, 52, has also made a career out of being an ex-tradwife, as a social media influencer and the author of two books about her experience. Like Gage, Levings married young, at 19, after which she and her husband moved around, and were part of several extreme, non-denominational fundamentalist Christian groups. One of these was the Institute in Basic Life Principles, which teaches that husbands have God-given authority over their wives, who in turn should not work outside the home and remain “well groomed” to “please their husbands”. It is an organisation that has faced allegations of misconduct – its founder, Bill Gothard, resigned in 2014 amid allegations of sexual abuse. It has also been alleged to have been “cult-like” by Jinger Duggar, a member of the family at the centre of the 00s reality TV show 19 Kids and Counting, who were members of the ministry.
Before social media, in the 00s, Levings was an early tradwife influencer on the blogosphere. At the time, her husband had moved their family into what she now describes as “a high-control family patriarchy cult”. On her blog, she wrote about “beautiful homey days and put pictures up of my cloth diapers and my beans and my bread”. She says that had she had social media then: “I definitely would have used it to do the same thing, to extol the virtues of this beautiful choice that you can make for your family.”
In reality, Levings’ life was neither virtuous nor beautiful. She says her husband abused her throughout their marriage and, because she had spent her whole life hearing that “divorce was wrong”, she was “too scared” to tell her parents or the authorities. The only person she felt she could approach was one of her church leaders: “What he told me was that I just needed to obey my husband more,” she says.
Levings says her husband’s behaviour became “much more violent” as the years went on and she was growing increasingly concerned that “I was teaching my children that it was OK for men to treat women this way.” She was also worried her family might not survive the violence. She knew she had to leave when her husband left the house suddenly in the middle of the night – she believes in order to retrieve his gun from his office – and she took the opportunity to flee. She now has custody of the couple’s four children.
When she looks back on her blogging days, she now sees how naive she was. “We join in, thinking: ‘Oh, we’re going to have a pretty family. We’re going to be happy traditional women,’” Levings says. What she wasn’t told was “what was also true of a traditional movement: here’s what happens when we don’t vaccinate kids. Here’s what happens when we take them out of education. Here’s what happens if your husband’s beating you and you can’t get out.”
Levings never thought she would go public with her story. But then she noticed the tradwife movement gaining traction on social media in about 2015 when Trump was first running for office. When figures in the American Christian right began to endorse Trump, Levings thought back to sermons she had listened to “where they were talking about taking away women’s rights to vote, taking away abortion, taking away education, turning America into a Christian nation”. She says: “I knew right away, this is the danger everyone’s in. And it was the moment I also understood that my lived experience was going to be relevant out here.”
Gage and Levings say their churches pushed white supremacist ideology. Levings recalls hearing a sermon on the “great replacement” theory as a child – which promotes the false idea that a group of Jews and Democrats is trying to “replace” white Americans with people of colour. Levings says she was told: “The way that we were going to fight that was by having as many white babies as possible.” They both now strongly renounce those views in their content.
Seyward Darby is the author of the 2020 book Sisters in Hate, about women on the frontline of white nationalist movements in the US. She says when she began researching her book in 2016, the first online performances of “trad life” online were “being really pushed by anti-feminists and also white nationalists”. Those origins might have become blurred in the years since, but “that’s still the DNA … so even though a tradwife today on TikTok might not say, ‘I’m a white nationalist,’ they might actually outright reject that, they’re still drawing on a trend that ultimately came from that space.” The tradwife aesthetic is seen as the perfect way to package extreme beliefs, says Darby, because of “the sexist assumption that women are nicer, women are softer” – so they become “the palatable faces of these rightwing movements”.

TEMPO.CO, Jakarta - Speaking alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Berlin on Tuesday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he had seen no sign that Russia is serious about negotiating a ceasefire in Ukraine.
Zelenskyy and Merz both said the European Union must help shape any lasting peace.
Germany expects European representatives to be in Abu Dhabi for next week's US-led talks with Ukraine and Russia, though they are unlikely to have a seat at the table.
"It is important that Russia finally and seriously engages in negotiations about a ceasefire and a subsequent peace agreement," Merz said when asked about the Abu Dhabi talks. "I do not see that happening so far."
Zelenskyy said he hopes the Abu Dhabi talks, the first trilateral sit down since February, could pave the way for a direct meeting between the Ukrainian president and Russia's Vladimir Putin, who has thus far refused several offers from Zelenskyy for face-to-face talks.
"We are counting on the fact that work in this format and our other diplomatic steps will open the way to a trilateral format at the level of leaders," he told reporters.
Europe must have a say on postwar security
Merz said Europe must have a say on sanctions and postwar security.
He said the local ceasefire in Oleshky could serve as a model for a wider truce, but warned that Russian attacks in the Black Sea risked further escalation. "Russia is precipitating a global food crisis, to the detriment of the poorest nations and countries in the world," he said.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine wanted a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure, safe passage for grain shipments through the Black Sea and further prisoner exchanges.
The Ukrainian president said a ceasefire alone would not secure a lasting peace. Ukraine would need security guarantees backed by Europe and the US. He insisted Europe must be involved in the negotiations.
"There cannot be a sustainable peace if Europe is not at the negotiating table," Zelenskyy said.
He said Ukraine would join the US, European partners and NATO for talks on security guarantees and reconstruction in Brussels on Wednesday.
Russia increases attacks on Ukrainian civilians
The talks in Berlin come as Russia continues to increase airstrikes on Ukrainian civilians.
Zelenskyy said at least 33 people were killed, and more than 50 could be trapped in rubble, after multiple Russian strikes on a school building used as an aid distribution center in the frontline southeastern village of on Monday.
Ukrainian officials said Russian forces launched an initial strike on residents waiting to receive aid, and then hit the same location again after waiting for rescue personnel to arrive on the scene, killing several of them and destroying emergency vehicles.
Speaking in Berlin, Zelenskyy described the strike as "one of the largest Russian killings of this war."
On Tuesday, at least 73 people were injured in a strike on a hospital in the northeastern city of Kharkiv, and 226 patients had to be transferred to other hospitals, regional prosecutors said.
Germany pledges aid ahead of winter
"Ahead of the next winter, air defense and the energy sector are our priorities," Merz said. He said Germany would soon deliver new aid in both areas and provide further winter assistance this year.
Zelenskyy thanked Germany for helping protect Ukraine's skies and supporting its energy infrastructure.
"Without Germany, we would not be as strong as we are," he said.
He said Ukraine urgently needed more air defense equipment, including Patriot interceptors.
Zelenskyy told EU leaders in October that Ukraine would need an additional €70 billion ($78 billion) from European governments next year. Germany plans to host a summit of countries backing Ukraine in mid-November to discuss further support ahead of winter.
How has Berlin stepped up security?
The visit coincides with the opening of the two-day Berlin Security Conference, which brings together European officials and defense experts. Russia's war in Ukraine is high on the agenda.
Police said about 3,400 additional officers were deployed for the visit and the conference, with reinforcements from across Germany.
Armed officers guarded barriers around parts of the government district, and special police units deployed snipers. Roads were also closed in western Berlin, including near the Kurfürstendamm shopping avenue.

articles.title: Iran plays down hope for deal to end war after new U.S. strikes on eve of midterm elections - CBS News
articles.summary: Iran plays down hope for deal to end war after new U.S. strikes on eve of midterm elections  CBS News
articles.full_text:
Follow . See earlier developments below.
What to know about the Iran war:
- A senior Iranian figure on Tuesday cast doubt on diplomatic efforts to broker a peace deal with the U.S., calling the Trump administration's response to the latest proposal "not convincing" and insisting that Iran's demands, including for a halt to fighting on all fronts in the Middle East, must be met if the Strait of Hormuz is to reopen.
- American forces near the strait on Monday, multiple U.S. officials told CBS News, in response to an apparent Iranian attack targeting a U.S. aircraft.
- President Trump said on the eve of that a deal with Iran to end the still "could happen," insisting Tehran "wants a settlement, as soon as possible."
Tanker hit by 2 projectiles off northeast coast of Oman, U.K. maritime agency says
Two unknown projectiles struck a tanker traveling near the northeast coast of Oman on Tuesday, according to a U.K. maritime agency.
The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations said it received a report from the tanker's security officer, who said the projectiles hit the vessel's engine room. It's not known who was operating the tanker in the Strait of Hormuz, where it came from or where it was headed.
No injuries or environmental impact had been reported, according to UKMTO.
"Vessels are advised to transit with caution and report any suspicious activity to UKMTO, whilst authorities investigate," the agency said.
Another vessel was also struck by an unknown projectile on Sunday near the same location.
Egyptian foreign minister urges "flexibility" in call with Iranian foreign minister
Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty asked Iran to show "flexibility" in negotiations Tuesday amid an apparent impasse with U.S. talks.
"I confirmed by phone with the Iranian Foreign Minister the necessity of exercising restraint and prioritizing diplomacy and negotiations, the importance of Gulf security, and showing flexibility to find a political way out and spare the region military escalation, which His Excellency President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi warned against its repercussions and political, economic, and security risks," Abdelatty said on X, translated from Arabic.
Egypt has tried to play mediator in the region as the conflict has continued to boil over in Iran, Gaza, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia and Yemen. An attack over the summer even targeted ships at a port in Egypt.
The call from Abdelatty about flexibility came on the same day the Iranians said they would only open the Strait of Hormuz and commit to peace talks if the U.S. followed Iran's seven-point plan.
Iran has continually pointed to the plan as the only way to move forward. However, the U.S. is unlikely to accept most of the points in that plan, including unfreezing assets, removing the blockade from Iranian ports, paying for damage caused in Iran by bombings and ending all military actions, including Israel's attacks in Lebanon.
Saudis intercept drone over eastern part of country
The Saudi-led coalition intercepted a drone over the eastern part of the country on Tuesday evening, according to spokesman Col. Turki Al-Malki.
The one-way attack drone was the second to be intercepted by coalition forces on Tuesday. An earlier drone was intercepted near the holy city of Mecca, though Houthi forces quickly denied the accusation. The Houthis have said publicly they will not target holy sites like Mecca.
There were no further details on the drone intercepted over the eastern part of Saudi Arabia, but the region is the hub of oil production in the country.
The headquarters of Saudi Aramco, the world's biggest oil company, are located in the eastern city of Dammam. Those headquarters, as well as the airport in Dammam, have been targeted multiple times by the Iran-backed Houthis. The airport, King Fahd International Airport, was targeted yesterday, the Houthis claimed.
Asian Cup soccer tournament latest sporting event in Saudi Arabia to be postponed due to war
The 2027 Asian Cup soccer tournament has been delayed almost a year in the wake of recent deadly attacks on host country Saudi Arabia, becoming the biggest sports event to be postponed amid the conflict in the Middle East.
The Asian Football Confederation issued a statement Tuesday that after consultations with Saudi organizers it decided to push the start of its marquee continental championship back from Jan. 7 to Dec. 23.
The decision came to seem likely after developments in recent weeks raised questions over whether the 2034 World Cup host nation is currently safe enough for a major international soccer tournament.
Several major sporting events have been postponed or canceled in Saudi Arabia due to Houthi attacks, including the Women's Tennis Association Finals, which were moved from Riyadh to Indian Wells, California, next week; and Netflix's Six Kings Slam tennis event, which was moved from late October to late December. Saudi Arabia's Formula 1 race was also canceled for the 2026 season back in April.
One exception is World Wrestling Entertainment, which will still be holding its Crown Jewel event in Riyadh this weekend.
CBS/AP
Higher oil prices boost Saudi Aramco profits despite disruption from Houthi attacks
The majority state-owned Saudi Aramco, the largest oil company in the world, on Tuesday reported a 35% increase in third-quarter net profit as earnings were boosted by higher oil prices and the sale of its stake in a Malaysian refining and petrochemical company.
Net profit rose to $36.3 billion from $26.9 billion in the year-earlier quarter. Adjusted net profit, which leaves out the sale of a stake in PRefChem to Malaysian state oil company Petronas, rose 9% to $31.2 billion.
The company also benefitted from high profit margins at its refineries turning crude into usable products such as diesel fuel.
Saudi Aramco sold its oil for an average of $95.20 a barrel during the quarter, compared to $70.10 in the year-before quarter, the company said in a news release. Oil prices surged after the outbreak of the Iran war due to disruption of supply and uncertainty about the course of the conflict.
After the war began, Saudi Aramco was able to use its East-West pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu to maintain a significant share of its oil exports despite disruption of tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz due to the risk of Iranian attack. The pipeline was attacked Sept. 10 but has since resumed flows.
Saudi oil is now also being transported through the strait using a U.S.-protected corridor near the coast of Oman. Exports have continued despite attacks on Aramco facilities by Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen.
AP/CBS
Islamic Revolutionary Guard says Iran will determine "time and conditions for ending the enemy's attacks"
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Tuesday that the country's armed forces and leadership would determine "the time and conditions for ending the enemy's attacks," after the U.S. carried out what American officials described to CBS News as limited, defensive strikes against Iranian targets on Monday.
In a statement conveyed by the Fars News agency, which is linked with the IRGC, the powerful paramilitary force said orders from Iran's supreme leader had been conveyed to senior military commanders, "in line with 'maximum deterrence' as our top priority, with full force, and we will not hesitate for a moment in implementing it."
The statement did not reveal any clear plans by Iran to retaliate for the latest U.S. strikes.
Senior Iranian official casts doubt on progress toward deal, calls U.S. response to demands "not convincing"
Senior Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei said Tuesday that the U.S. response to "Iran's rights and demands was not convincing," suggesting ongoing efforts by mediators Qatar and Pakistan to broker an agreement between Washington and Tehran still had significant hurdles to overcome.
"America's response to Iran's rights and demands was not convincing, and they must fully and explicitly address Iran's seven conditions and act upon them; only in this case will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened," Rezaei, Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council of Iran, said in a post on X.
Senior figures in the Iranian regime have stressed for weeks that any agreement with the U.S. to end the war would require Washington to meet demands including a complete cessation of hostilities not only in the Persian Gulf, but in Lebanon and the Gaza Strip, as well as lifting the U.S. blockade of Iran's ports and unfreeing Iranian financial assets held outside the country.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baqaei told reporters later Tuesday that Iran was "not afraid of diplomacy," provided that it was used to "safeguard the interests of the Iranian nation and prevent the escalation of insecurity in the region."
"Given the United States' record of violating previous agreements, we participate in any diplomatic process with the utmost caution and complete distrust," Baqaei said. "Reaching any understanding is conditional on an unequivocal commitment to stopping the war on all fronts, including Lebanon."
U.K. navy agency says attack hit small Indian-crewed vessel in Strait of Hormuz
The U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said Tuesday that it was "aware of a report by the Indian Government of an attack on an Indian crewed Dhow whilst sailing outbound through the Strait of Hormuz," seemingly confirming a strike that killed at least one mariner earlier in the day, but clarifying that it was a small vessel, not a large cargo ship.
Indian Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal said earlier that the MSV Al Jusufi, which he described as a cargo vessel, had 14 Indian seafarers on board when it was attacked.
"While 13 crew members safely evacuated and were rescued by the Omani Coast Guard, I am deeply saddened to report that one of our seafarers, Gandhar Nahim Ajij from Gujarat, tragically succumbed to his injuries," Sonowal said in a statement on social media.
No one immediately claimed

articles.summary: UK Cyber Chief Warns of Unprecedented Threat as Hostile Nations Weaponize AI  NTD News
articles.full_text:
Organizations across the United Kingdom face a critical window to overhaul their digital defenses or risk catastrophic losses, as artificial intelligence accelerates the speed and scale of global cyberattacks.
According to the report, it is "highly likely" that ransomware syndicates will weaponize artificial intelligence within the UK. Simultaneously, hostile nation-states—including Russia and China—are leveraging advanced AI tools to advance strategic objectives and conduct foreign interference.
The warning follows a wave of coordinated attacks across Europe. Hackers recently gained remote control of commercial refrigeration systems across Belgium, Sweden, Luxembourg, Finland, Ireland, Estonia, and the UK, raising temperatures and causing widespread food spoilage. Similar breaches targeted French supermarkets and food distributors in early October, inflicting millions of euros in damages.
Horne emphasized that legacy technology across public and private sectors has left systemic vulnerabilities exposed. AI does not necessarily invent novel attack vectors; instead, it allows adversaries to automate the discovery and exploitation of long-tolerated security flaws at unprecedented speed.
"In the coming months, we face a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents," Horne warned, describing the convergence of systemic vulnerabilities and rapid AI growth as a moment of "enormous consequence."
To counter these threats, Horne called on executive leadership to reverse decades of systemic underinvestment in foundational IT infrastructure.
“For decades, we have collectively got away with doing tech on the cheap,” Horne remarked. “We can be a nation where leaders of all organizations actively choose to invest with urgency ... and where all organizations make security and resilience a fundamental requirement, not an afterthought.”
He cautioned that executives who neglect cyber resilience will ultimately have to look their investors, shareholders, employees, customers, and suppliers in the eye when operational failures disrupt essential services.
Underscoring the broader risk to national resilience, UK Health Secretary Wes Streeting separately advised the public to keep basic reserves of food and water to prepare for potential power outages or national emergencies.
China-Linked AI Cyber Campaign
The NCSC alert comes on the heels of a massive mid-October cyber campaign in which threat actors deployed AI tools to target hundreds of sensitive organizations globally across defense, energy, finance, government, and technology sectors.
Microsoft reported that China-affiliated hackers have used AI since at least September of last year to breach cloud environments, occasionally gaining administrative control in under three hours.
In response, the UK government is committing targeted funding to enhance defense capabilities. The newly announced National Cyber Shield initiative will receive £60 million to integrate AI into national defensive operations, alongside an additional £70 million allocated toward developing automated diagnostic tools to detect vulnerabilities across critical infrastructure.

Key Highlights:
- The UK’s NCSC says an AI-based cyberattack on critical national infrastructure is highly likely by 2028.
- China is considered the country best positioned to use AI in cyber operations against Britain’s strategic targets, while Russia and Iran also pose cybersecurity concerns.
- NCSC Chief Executive Richard Horne has urged organisations to address longstanding technology and security weaknesses before they are exploited at scale.
The United Kingdom is facing an escalating cybersafety threat as AI makes it easier for hostile actors to identify and exploit vulnerabilities in digital systems. The National Cyber Security Centre ( NCSC) has advised that Britain should brace for an AI-based cyberattack. The attack will target critical national infrastructure within the next two years. The warning emphasizes concerns about weaknesses across essential services, businesses and technology supply chains that could become susceptible to AI-based attacks.
NCSC Chief Executive Richard Horne has urged organizations to strengthen cybersecurity measures, warning that years of underinvestment has left parts of Britain’s digital infrastructure exposed.
Why is the UK Warning About AI-Based Cyberattacks?
In its yearly report, the NCSC said it was highly possible that a ransomware attack involving AI malware would occur against Britain’s critical infrastructure by 2028. The agency also advised that hostile actors were expected to use AI to increase the magnitude of their cyber activities during the same period. Richard Horne, chief executive of the NCSC said organisations and supply chains had spent substantial amounts of time depending on poor technology and cybersecurity investments.
He argued that too many businesses had effectively been “doing tech on the cheap”, leaving weaknesses that attackers could exploit. “In the coming months, we face a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents,” Horne is expected to say in his speech.
Britain should be prepared for an AI-powered cyberattack on its critical national infrastructure in the next two years, the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre said, adding that China was likely the best equipped to conduct such operations https://t.co/chzxx5XfYq
— Reuters (@Reuters) November 3, 2026
However, he stressed that AI was not necessarily creating entirely new methods of cyberattacks. Instead, the technology was making it feasible to identify and nitpick weaknesses easily. But we must be clear that is not because AI has invented new ways to attack us, but because vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long can now be discovered and exploited at a scale that was once unimaginable,” he said.
Which Countries Does the NCSC Identify as Major Cybersecurity Threats?
The NCSC identifies China of being the most significant state-linked cybersecurity challenge facing the UK. They argue that Beijing has both the intention and technical capabilities to use AI against critical national infrastructure and other strategic targets.
“We know that China highly likely has the intent and is best positioned to use AI for operations against our critical national infrastructure and other strategic targets with their activity representing the most sophisticated and sustained cyber challenge the UK faces,” Horne is expected to say.
The report also talked about cyber operations associated with Russia and Iran. Horne said Russia was making sustained attempts to penetrate British military networks, while Iran was conducting malicious cyber activities globally, including against the UK and individuals it considers threats. However, the evaluation does not indicate that every cyber incident targeting Britain will necessarily be state-sponsored or AI-based cyberattack. Rather, it points to the growing range of threats facing the country’s digital infrastructure.
Horne said organisations needed to take action before weaknesses resulted in serious consequences. He advised that businesses could eventually be forced to explain why they ignored known risks if cyberattacks caused food shortages, power disruptions or business failures. His message was that firms already have enough context to understand the threat and should not wait for a major incident before improving their security.
The warning places extra pressure on British conglomerates to strengthen their technology infrastructure, review supply-chain security and brace for attacks that could become swifter and more sophisticated through artificial intelligence.

articles.title: NCSC warns of ‘unprecedented’ rise in cyber incidents, even as serious breaches fall - Insurance Business
articles.summary: NCSC warns of ‘unprecedented’ rise in cyber incidents, even as serious breaches fall  Insurance Business
articles.full_text:
The head of the National Cyber Security Centre has warned that the UK faces a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in cyber incidents in the coming months. His warning came on the same day his agency reported a sharp fall in the most serious attacks.
Richard Horne was speaking at today’s launch of the NCSC’s 2026 annual review. He said the problem was not that AI had invented new ways to attack organisations. It was that weaknesses tolerated for years can now be found and exploited at a scale nobody previously thought possible.
“For decades, we have collectively got away with doing tech on the cheap,” he said.
The numbers in the review tell a more mixed story. Between September 2025 and August 2026, the NCSC received 1,831 reports of attacks on UK organisations, up from 1,727 a year earlier. It gave hands-on support in 337 cases, down from 429, and classed 80 as nationally significant. A year ago that figure was 204, or about four a week. This year it is closer to one and a half.
The NCSC does not treat the fall as a trend - the review says incident numbers rarely move in a straight line and that past peaks were often caused by a handful of severe events. Its verdict on the country’s defences does not make cheery reading: “The UK’s cyber resilience is not yet where it should be.”
That message is arriving as cyber rates have been falling for nearly three years. A lower count of major incidents is an easy number to bring to a renewal meeting. Horne’s speech and the review behind it suggest the underlying risk is moving the other way.
Horne said leaders who keep putting off investment, may end up explaining to investors, staff, customers and suppliers why food is not on the shelves, the lights are off and businesses have collapsed.
He also urged organisations to stop connecting technology to the internet when it doesn’t need to be. And he called on them to treat Cyber Essentials as the starting point for their security, building further protection according to their size, complexity and risk.
The NCSC judges it highly likely that by 2028, China, Russia and other states will routinely use AI in cyber operations against the UK. It also judges it highly likely that AI-powered malware will be used in a ransomware attack on UK critical national infrastructure within the same period.
Read next: Inside the cyber gap: Why major UK firms are still underinsured and unprepared
For now, attackers are mostly getting in the way they always have. Among large organisations, 88% of the incidents the NCSC handled began in one of four ways: exploiting a public-facing application, phishing, misusing a legitimate account or exploiting remote access services. The incident team has seen AI tools in use, but none of them enabled a new type of attack.
The biggest concern is how fast this could happen. The NCSC expects AI models to uncover large numbers of previously unknown flaws in widely used software. It has told organisations to prepare for a “vulnerability patch wave”: a rush of urgent updates across the technology they rely on.
A burst of exploitable flaws in common software could hit many policyholders at once, which makes it an aggregation problem as well as a frequency one.
The review also flags “shadow AI”, where staff put company data into unapproved AI tools, often on personal devices. Questions about it are likely to start appearing on proposal forms.
The review calls China the most sophisticated and sustained cyber threat the UK faces, and Russia the most audacious. It points to a December 2025 attack on Poland’s energy grid, which the UK and EU attributed to a unit of Russia’s FSB. Had it succeeded, around 500,000 people could have lost power.
For insurers, this keeps state-backed attacks and the wording of war and state-actor exclusions firmly on the agenda. The more cyber operations become part of ordinary geopolitical pressure, the harder it gets to draw a clean line between a criminal loss and a state-sponsored one.
The NCSC uses the 2025 attack on Jaguar Land Rover as its main example of economic harm. JLR reported about £196m in direct costs. The review links the incident to UK growth of just 0.1% in the third quarter of 2025, below forecasts.
Insurance gets no mention. But JLR had not completed its Lockton-brokered cyber placement when the attack hit. The review’s account of suppliers losing orders and payments while production stopped describes the contingent business interruption risk that insurers have since begun to cover.
The review also repeats a government estimate that cyber attacks cost UK organisations about £14.7bn a year. That is roughly the size of the UK’s entire cyber security sector.
Read next: Did Jaguar Land Rover’s cyber insurance gap help pave the way to 4,000 job losses?
Take-up of basic controls is still rising. In the 12 months to August, 47,661 Cyber Essentials certificates were awarded, up 19.6%. Cyber Essentials Plus certificates rose 21.5% to 15,646. The NCSC’s free Early Warning service, which alerts organisations to suspicious activity on their networks, now has 19,922 organisations signed up, a 52% increase.
The government says certified organisations are 92% less likely to make a claim on their cyber insurance. The figure is based on data from the insurer that provides the free cover bundled with certification.
The harder job is reaching everyone else. Government survey data found that 47% of UK businesses have cyber cover in any form, and standalone policies are far less common. The NCSC warns of a widening gap between organisations that can afford modern, AI-assisted defences and those stuck with old systems. For insurers, that means two quite different groups of risks sitting under the same product line.
Read next: Brit cyber cover now available through Acturis package placements
Horne’s speech gives brokers a ready-made line for client meetings: Cyber Essentials is where security starts, not where it ends. For eligible UK firms with turnover under £20m, whole-organisation certification also lets them opt into included cyber insurance. That can open a conversation about whether the cover is anywhere near enough.
Early Warning is free and is an easy recommendation at renewal. The NCSC’s new guidance on recovering from a highly disruptive cyber attack, written with boards in mind, is worth putting in front of any client who treats their policy as their recovery plan.
According to the NCSC, the Chancellor announced new funding last week for AI-driven cyber defence:
Security minister Dan Jarvis also points to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, which is still going through Parliament. It would bring managed service providers and other sectors into regulation and give ministers new powers during national security crises. The Association of British Insurers has backed the bill, citing nearly £200m in cyber claims paid in a single year.
Read next: ABI backs UK Cyber Security Bill as insurers brace for rising demand
The NCSC’s figures show a quieter year for the most serious attacks. Its chief executive is warning that the next one is unlikely to stay that way.

articles.title: Trump's Iran dilemma as Americans vote: escalate, negotiate or risk wider war - The National
articles.summary: Trump's Iran dilemma as Americans vote: escalate, negotiate or risk wider war  The National
articles.full_text:
US midterm elections could shape the next phase of the conflict with Iran, with a Republican loss potentially constraining Mr Trump's military and funding options.
Washington struck Iran's Qeshm Island on election day, destroying a surface-to-air missile launcher after Tehran claimed to have downed an American drone.
CIA director John Ratcliffe is advising Mr Trump to maintain a "no war, no deal" status quo, believing prolonged economic pressure could force Iranian concessions.
US weapons stockpiles have been significantly depleted, with Thaad interceptors down 80 per cent and Patriot interceptors reduced by 65 per cent, complicating renewed military action.
"Iran has made a big gamble by dragging out the war until the US midterm elections, hoping to buy time," said a senior Iran analyst at Dawn.
Americans will vote on Tuesday in midterm elections that could shape the next phase of the war with Iran, as US President Donald Trump considers whether to resume a major military campaign, with diplomacy yet to produce a breakthrough.
The war has become an increasingly heavy political burden for the White House, as the conflict is blamed for higher prices of fuel, housing and groceries that have affected millions of voters.
Analysts say a Republican loss of either the Senate or House of Representatives would constrain Mr Trump's options, making it harder to secure funding and sustain political support for renewed military action, although he could still order further strikes.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pressing Mr Trump to resume military action against Iran after the midterms, including strikes on its underground nuclear infrastructure at Pickaxe Mountain.
Washington is meanwhile limiting military action while pursuing negotiations.
The attack in the Strait of Hormuz appeared limited in scope, involving a single US fighter jet that destroyed an Iranian surface-to-air missile launcher, and came after Iran claimed to have shot down an American MQ-9 Reaper drone east of the strait.
The developments underline the dilemma facing Mr Trump on election day: whether limited military pressure can strengthen Washington’s negotiating position, or if such a move would lead to another escalation without delivering a peace settlement.
The timing has also raised questions.
Sina Toossi, a senior fellow at the Centre for International Policy, asked why US officials were publicising supposedly “secret” strikes just as Mr Trump was touting diplomatic progress and falling oil prices, and whether the disclosures were an attempt to “project toughness for political optics” before the vote.
Election pressure
Iran may also be calculating that prolonging the conflict will increase the political cost for the US President.
“Iran has made a big gamble by dragging out the war until the US midterm elections, hoping to buy time,” Omid Memarian, senior Iran analyst at the democracy and human rights organisation Dawn, told The National.
Rising living costs could leave Mr Trump facing a steep political price if Republicans lose control of either chamber of Congress. “That would make it harder for him to continue the war, secure funding for it, and justify further military attacks,” he said.
He warned that Mr Trump was not a conventional president and could still take unexpected decisions. Nevertheless, losing the House would create serious domestic problems. The election could therefore increase pressure on Mr Trump to end the conflict, although that does not rule out further military action.
There are differing views within the administration. CIA director John Ratcliffe is advising Mr Trump to maintain the “no war, no deal” status quo and allow the economic pressure campaign to continue, Axios reported. His assessment is that prolonged economic pain could force Tehran to make further concessions or generate enough domestic instability to provoke an uprising.
Diplomatic opening
The latest contacts have produced a draft proposal, but no agreement. Iranian negotiators left Doha after three days of discussions, while Qatari mediators have returned to Tehran to continue consultations.
Mr Trump has said a deal remained possible. “It could happen,” he told reporters on Monday, without providing details.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the President had set no deadline for negotiations and had made no decision on further strikes. “If there is a diplomatic solution, we would be open to it,” Mr Rubio said. He added that any agreement must address Washington’s core security concerns and that the US retained the military capability to act if diplomacy failed.
A letter from Vice President JD Vance to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council of Iran, has also opened another channel, although Tehran has yet to send a formal reply.
The Qatari initiative centres on a draft agreement based on Iran’s seven-step proposal to end the war. Under its terms, Washington would end its blockade of Iranian ports, Tehran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and the US would ease restrictions on Iranian oil sales and impose no new sanctions. Discussions on other issues would follow.
The gaps remain substantial. Iran wants sanctions relief and an end to the blockade before substantive nuclear negotiations, while Washington wants verifiable concessions on Tehran’s nuclear programme and wider security concerns.
Military options carry wider costs
US weapons inventories have been depleted, with reports that stocks of Thaad interceptors have fallen by as much as 80 per cent and Patriot interceptors by up to 65 per cent. Tomahawk cruise missile inventories have also been significantly reduced. Further fighting would add to the financial cost of a conflict estimated at about $47 billion.
Iran, meanwhile, does not need to match American military capabilities to impose costs. Missile and drone attacks, threats to US installations and disruption of commercial shipping could force Washington and its regional partners to expend expensive defensive weapons, and could threaten energy infrastructure and trade.
A renewed campaign could hit remaining nuclear sites, missile and drone capabilities or other military infrastructure. But destroying sites would not necessarily eliminate Iran’s nuclear expertise, secure its remaining enriched uranium or prevent it from rebuilding capabilities elsewhere.
Unresolved threat
The stakes for regional governments were underlined by Amos Hochstein, a senior adviser in former US president Joe Biden’s administration, who warned that Washington could leave the Iranian regime “angry and vengeful” and a continuing threat to its Gulf allies unless the conflict is brought to a clear end.
Speaking in Abu Dhabi on Sunday to Hadley Gamble’s On the Record, which airs on The National and Sky News Arabia, he urged the Trump administration to pursue a negotiated settlement. He said he had supported Mr Trump’s June 2025 strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities but opposed the current war.
Military analyst Lynette Nusbacher also questioned whether air strikes could achieve a lasting political outcome.
“They will not cause people to change their government, and we’ve seen that the Iranian state is configured precisely to withstand this kind of attack,” she told The National.
For Gulf states, the continued disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz is threatening energy exports and trade, while attacks on infrastructure could undermine the region’s ambitions as a centre for investment, trade, aviation and finance.

articles.title: The Leadership Trap in European Defense - Small Wars Journal
articles.summary: The Leadership Trap in European Defense  Small Wars Journal
articles.full_text:
Abstract
For decades, debate surrounding European defense has focused predominantly on capability shortfalls, defense spending targets, and burden-sharing metrics within NATO. However, contemporary security literature demonstrates that the principal vulnerability of European security is not merely a quantitative deficit in military hardware, but a qualitative and structural dependency on United States strategic leadership. This paper argues that European Allies face a profound challenge of leadership dependency; a systemic reliance on U.S. threat assessment, political initiative, operational planning, and crisis decision-making. Transitioning toward a sustainable model of European security requires moving beyond capability accumulation to foster strategic leadership, institutional agility, and political initiative. By examining the institutional friction points between NATO and the EU, the psychological dynamics of the “follower mentality,” the dependence on strategic enablers, and the imperatives of European-led interoperability, this study outlines a strategic framework for cultivating autonomous European defense leadership as a complementary pillar within the Atlantic Alliance.
Introduction: The Leadership Paradox in European Defense
The central dilemma facing contemporary European security is no longer whether Europe must assume greater responsibility for the continent’s defense, but whether Europe and NATO can develop the strategic leadership, political will, and institutional capacity to act proactively rather than remain structurally dependent on American initiative. For nearly eight decades, transatlantic defense discourse has operated within a well-rehearsed framework centered on burden-sharing metrics. From the 2014 NATO Wales Summit target of spending 2% of GDP on defense to subsequent procurement benchmarks, the debate has treated European strategic weakness as a primary function of resource underinvestment. While capital investment and force modernization remain indispensable, this emphasis obscures a deeper, more pervasive vulnerability: strategic leadership dependency. As the European Council concluded during a strategic discussion held on June 2023 and March 2024 regarding European security readiness, “The defense of Europe requires a comprehensive concept of security… enhanced and coordinated military and civil preparedness and strategic crisis management are required.”
Given these imperatives and Europe’s ongoing institutional coordination challenges, increasing defense expenditure, procuring advanced military platforms, and expanding force structures do not, in themselves, resolve Europe’s structural dependency on the United States. Moreover, strategic leadership requires the capacity to identify emerging threats, establish strategic priorities, formulate political decisions under time pressure, generate viable military options, and command complex multinational operations, including in scenarios where U.S. engagement is limited, delayed, or redirected.
Figure 1: Leader -Follower model vs Strategic model
As illustrated in Figure 1, understanding this challenge necessitates distinguishing between reducing U.S. responsibility and Europeanizing security leadership. The objective of European strategic autonomy or Europeanized defense within NATO is not to supplant or exclude the United States. Rather, it is to transform a leader-follower dynamic into a balanced partnership of complementary leadership responsibilities. Without a fundamental change in strategic culture, political decision-making mechanics, and operational frameworks, increased European defense spending risks producing larger supporting forces rather than self-directed strategic actors.
The Anatomy of Leadership Dependency
To understand the institutional and psychological barriers to European strategic action, we must dissect the mechanisms through which U.S. leadership dependency became embedded in the transatlantic alliance architecture.
Figure 2: Dimensions of Leadership Dependency
As illustrated in Figure 2, European strategic reliance operates across five core dimensions: strategic culture, intelligence assessment, high-end enablers, operational interoperability, and institutional decision-making. Each dimension presents a distinct vulnerability, ranging from waiting for U.S. consensus and relying on American intelligence feeds to persistent gaps in ISR, space, airlift, and decision-making bottlenecks during rapid-onset crises. Together, these structural manifestations reinforce a systemic leader-follower dynamic where Europe frequently follows rather than takes the lead in its own regional security.
2.1 The Long-Standing U.S.-Led Security Model
Since the signing of the North Atlantic Treaty in 1949, NATO’s strategic direction, military innovation, operational planning, intelligence architecture, high-end enablers, and crisis-response mechanisms have been shaped predominantly by the United States. European allies entered into a structural contract: the United States provided the ultimate nuclear deterrent, advanced command-and-control (C2), strategic intelligence, and global operational enablers, while European allies provided forward-deployed ground forces, localized air defense, and basing infrastructure.
This strategic dependency is further exacerbated by an over reliance on off-the-shelf American defense platforms, as evidenced by European states directing the vast majority of their capability investment budgets toward U.S. military hardware, specifically high-tier acquisitions such as F-35 fighter aircraft, Patriot missile defense batteries, and Tomahawk missiles, rather than sovereign European alternatives.
This dependency is most acute in operational command-and-control (C2) and strategic intelligence. Despite substantial European aid to Ukraine, target generation, situational awareness, and theater-level coordination remain fundamentally anchored to U.S. C2 networks and intelligence platforms. The war in Ukraine has shown that Europe still lacks a standalone, campaign-level joint command structure, leaving allies structurally dependent on Washington for operational direction and execution
Over decades, this division of labor institutionalized a division of intellectual and operational responsibility. The U.S. assumed the role of strategic initiator, threat-framer, and operational architect, while European allies operated as force providers and supporters. Consequently, European defense planning developed reactively, aligning national force structures to fit into U.S.-designed operational frameworks rather than preparing for independent strategic action.
2.2 The Psychological Dimension and the “Follower Mentality”
The most stubborn obstacle to European strategic leadership is not material, but psychological and cultural. Decades of structural reliance have fostered a “follower mentality” across European political elites, civil services, and military staffs.
When faced with emerging crises, whether in the Balkans, Eastern Europe, the Middle East, or the Mediterranean, the default strategic question in European capitals has consistently been: “What will the United States do?” This orientation reflects an entrenched habit of waiting for Washington to provide threat assessments, establish political consensus, and propose operational options.
Moving toward European leadership requires shifting the foundational strategic question to: “What should Europe do, and what role should the United States play?” This conceptual realignment represents a profound shift in strategic culture. Culture cannot be updated through budget allocations or equipment purchases; it requires deliberate institutional habits, routine exercise of independent responsibility, and a willingness to accept political risk.
2.3 Leadership versus Capability
A central fallacy in contemporary defense policy is the assumption that capability automatically yields leadership. While military capabilities represent the necessary muscle of strategy, leadership represents the central nervous system. Possessing advanced fighter aircraft, armored brigades, or naval combatants does not grant a nation or coalition the capacity to act autonomously if those forces cannot be directed, sustained, or employed without external strategic direction.
Figure 3: Strategic Leadership
As illustrated in Figure 3, achieving true strategic leadership requires far more than quantitative defense capabilities, combining raw hardware and funding with proactive threat assessment, streamlined political decision-making, and high-end operational enablers. Only by integrating all four pillars can European allies build the unified command structures, strategic vision, and power projection needed to set direction and independently lead regional defense.
Coalition Strategic leadership requires:
- Intellectual Autonomy: The capability to conduct independent strategic reconnaissance, synthesis, and threat assessment.
- Political Decisiveness: The ability to navigate divergent national interests to formulate timely collective decisions.
- Operational Command: The capacity to plan, command, and sustain high-intensity, multi-domain joint operations across extended timelines.

The drums of war are once again sounding across the Middle East.
Tucker Carlson, the former Fox News presenter and Maga whisperer, claimed on Monday that sources within the Trump administration, including Pete Hegseth, the US defence secretary, were considering a nuclear strike on Iran.
“Under pressure from Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the Trump administration may be within days of launching a nuclear strike on Iran,” he said in a social media post. “The target would be Pickaxe Mountain in central Iran, where Israeli intelligence claims the Iranian government has restarted its nuclear enrichment program.”
The claims from the journalist and provocateur have been widely derided, but analysts say there is no doubt that the US is planning, in co-operation with Israel, a third major wave of military strikes against Iran.
On Monday night, Donald Trump did not shy away from the prospect of at least some form of strike on the underground nuclear facility.
“We might have to go after Pickaxe, but that’s not a big deal,” he told Fox News. “We can do it in literally one hour.”
Then, the US launched new strikes on Iran, targeting Qeshm Island in what Pentagon officials indicated was part of a series of small-scale defensive strikes which did not signify a return to all-out conflict.
Diplomacy is also in overdrive, with Qatar acting as the principal mediator between the US and Iran, and JD Vance, the US vice-president, leading the American side.
A peaceful solution therefore cannot be ruled out. However, if talks once again fail, a new shooting war is likely. These are Donald Trump’s main options, rated in terms of likelihood:
1/10: A US tactical nuclear strike on Pickaxe Mountain
Mr Carlson, somewhat improbably, suggested a tactical nuclear strike on Pickaxe Mountain was being considered by the White House under “maximum pressure” from the Israeli prime minister.
The idea, said Mr Carlson, without providing evidence, would be to use a nuclear weapon to destroy the site of Iran’s nuclear programme. This, he argued, was the only weapon that could reach the underground fortress and destroy it because it was buried beneath up to 100m of hard granite.

articles.title: After midterm loss, Trump is left to weigh his next move in Iran war that contributed to GOP debacle - Bozeman Daily Chronicle
articles.summary: After midterm loss, Trump is left to weigh his next move in Iran war that contributed to GOP debacle  Bozeman Daily Chronicle
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — As he takes stock of his Republican Party's midterm drubbing, President Donald Trump now faces the difficult question of what to do about his unpopular 8-month-old war against Iran.
For weeks, Trump has threatened to return to a full-scale bombardment of Iran once the U.S. elections were in the rearview mirror if Tehran did not come to a settlement under terms acceptable to him.
In his first comments on Wednesday after Democrats' resounding election victory — a wave powered in part by the American electorate's dissatisfaction with the war — Trump largely agreed with Vice President JD Vance, who publicly ruminated on the war being a catastrophe for Republicans.
“It’s largely true because it drove gasoline up a little bit,” Trump said. Still, he doubled down on his decision to launch the conflict despite its big political cost. “At the same time, if I had to do it again, I'd do it again," he said.
The strikes, and counterstrikes, have caused tens of billions of dollars of damage in the region. And the conflict has reached into the pocketbook of families around the globe with elevated gas prices and rising costs in just about every sector.
Now, as Trump ponders his next move, the stakes couldn't be higher for Iran, the Middle East and the global economy writ large.
Trump may be less restrained, but the conflict is now more complicated
While oil is flowing again from the Strait of Hormuz with the help of U.S. Navy escorts for international tankers, the conflict has spread to the Red Sea with Iran-backed Houthi rebels and a Saudi Arabia -led coalition fighting it out.
The situation in the Red Sea remains particularly volatile. The Houthis are attacking Yemeni civilians and Saudi infrastructure, and are looking to bolster ties with militant groups across the Horn of Africa.
The attacks by the Yemen-based Houthis on areas controlled by the internationally recognized Yemeni government have also worsened a growing humanitarian crisis.
The threat that the region faces from Iran and its proxy groups, noted a senior Yemeni government official, “did not change overnight” with the U.S. elections, urging Washington to avoid hasty decisions. The official was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the basis of anonymity.
“There’s reason to suspect that Trump may feel less restrained given that the political damage is done,” said Brian Haggerty, a former senior analyst at the Central Intelligence Agency who focused on Middle East security issues. “At the same time, the strategic calculus or the strategic logic of what you hope to achieve through an escalation of strikes against Iran is no different today than it was a week ago or a month ago.”
Trump has at least a few options, analysts say
Haggerty, who now works with Defense Priorities, a Washington think tank, said Trump could choose to maintain something close to the current posture, with the U.S. military carrying out what it calls “defensive strikes” while continuing its naval blockade to restrict the flow of Iranian oil to the global market.
Another option is striking Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to its nuclear program that is buried deep underground in central Iran, said David Schenker, who served as assistant secretary of state for Near Eastern affairs in Trump’s first term. Trump has repeatedly suggested he was considering targeting the site.
Schenker said Trump could then walk away and contend he had done sufficient damage to Iran's nuclear program — and perhaps try to pursue a “fig leaf agreement” that restores freedom of navigation to the Strait of Hormuz, offers Iran some degree of sanctions relief, and punts additional nuclear talks to the future.
Yet another option would be to follow up on threats Trump made earlier in the war to launch massive attacks on Iranian infrastructure. “The Iranians may believe the president is wounded and constrained by Congress, but the opposite can also be true,” Schenker said.
But such escalation would likely exacerbate the oil and energy price problem that many voters cited as a reason for supporting Democrats on Tuesday, Schenker said.
The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil tumbled below $95 on Wednesday after the election, touching its lowest level in two months, a signal that markets do not expect major strikes.
Regional officials are on high alert for what Trump does next
Middle East officials had been hanging on Trump’s every word in the weeks leading up to the U.S. elections, looking for clues on how the Republican leader was weighing his next steps.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pressed for renewed strikes on Iran during a call over the weekend with Trump, who would not commit to taking military action, according to a person who was briefed on it.
Three Middle Eastern government officials said on Wednesday that Trump and his administration had seemed to be signaling to Iran that its leverage would only diminish after the U.S. elections were over.
Administration officials had privately suggested in diplomatic channels that Trump might be more willing to restart strikes after Nov. 3 because he'd have little left to lose politically, according to the officials, who were not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
After Tuesday’s electoral shellacking, there was lingering concern that Trump might be more emboldened to carry out full-scale or new limited strikes against Iran, the officials said.
A fourth official said the results of the election gave mediators a measure of optimism about finding a pathway to resolving the conflict.
Meanwhile, Vance appeared to more forcefully pin the electoral debacle on the Iran war than his boss Trump, who initially blamed the GOP's candidates for the big loss.
“The reason we lost,” Vance said of the midterm elections in a lengthy social media post, “is the war.”
Vance, a potential 2028 presidential contender, had been among the most skeptical inside the White House on the wisdom of launching the war but got on board with Trump's decision once he made it.
Voter data shows Iran had an impact but was not the top issue
Several Democratic candidates who scored upsets on Tuesday noted voter discontent with the Iran war in their victory speeches.
“Wherever I went, I heard the same thing,” said Sen.-elect Josh Turek of Iowa. “They would say, Josh, I’m struggling just to keep food on the table, keep a roof above my head, pay my electric bill. And with this war in Iran, I’m struggling just to keep gas in my tank.”
About 6 in 10 voters said the U.S. made the “wrong decision” in taking military action against Iran, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 voters in the United States.
Most of those voters dissatisfied with the Iran war backed the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race, but the survey suggested the Iran war was not the top issue for most voters.
Only about one-third of voters said the war in Iran was “crucial” to shaping how they voted for Congress. That was well below the roughly half who said that about the cost of living or government corruption.
Nearly all voters who backed the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race said going to war with Iran was the “wrong decision,” while roughly 8 in 10 voters who backed the Republican candidate said it was the “right decision.”
Meanwhile, about 6 in 10 voters nationally said they were “very concerned” about the cost of gasoline and diesel, the poll showed — and about two-thirds of that group voted for the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race.
But Trump, for his part, said even in hindsight he'd approach Iran exactly as he has.
“I can tell you that as far as that war is concerned I would have done nothing different," the president said.
Magdy reported from New York. AP writers Collin Binkley in Washington, Hannah Fingerhut in Des Moines, Iowa, and Kathleen Foody in Chicago contributed reporting.
