articles.title: The Dangers of a Lame-Duck Trump
articles.summary: How far will he go to make peace—and war?
articles.full_text:
With the midterms over, U.S. President Donald Trump is now a lame duck. Second-term presidents who lose control of Congress have to face the reality that the time for signature legislation or other domestic policy initiatives has passed. As they think about their legacy, lame ducks often turn to foreign policy, where the power of the presidency allows them to act unfettered by pesky domestic politics. It is not unusual for a lame duck to reach for a final, lofty goal abroad. U.S. President Bill Clinton, for instance, put great effort into trying to advance a proposal for a final settlement to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict at the end of his presidency.
Trump’s lame-duck period will not be like those of his predecessors, however. He has already gone through what was widely considered at the time to be a lame-duck phase, between November 2020 and January 2021. He used it to contest the election outcome despite clear evidence that Joe Biden had won. Trump is the first president in the past 100 years to have served two nonconsecutive terms, and therefore the only American leader in living memory to have a second lame-duck period—this time lasting more than two years.
With Democrats soon to be in control of the House and the Senate, the threat of impeachment or investigations into the Trump family’s business dealings will likely make the president feel cornered and angry. And that’s what makes the remainder of Trump’s term so dangerous. A boxed-in Trump, with no obvious constructive foreign policy outlet to channel his energy, may well lash out internationally. And Congress, even if controlled by Democrats, will have little power over his day-to-day management of foreign policy.
There are plenty of ways Trump could act out: issuing fresh threats against Canada, launching new attacks on U.S. alliances, or colluding with Russia or China at the expense of Ukraine or Taiwan. But to turn those threats into policy would require serious effort, such as repositioning U.S. troops or painstakingly negotiating with other great powers.
The two places where Trump can inflict the most damage are Iran and Cuba. According to The New York Times, the Trump administration and Israel have drawn up plans for fresh strikes on Iran as soon as the midterms are over. A last-ditch effort to compel Tehran to surrender is unlikely to work and would put at risk the global economy and the security and stability of Persian Gulf allies. Trump might also try to force regime change in Cuba. Military action against both adversaries would only require Trump to give his say-so. With no election on the horizon, all that constrains the president abroad is the sense of his own legacy.
ONE FOOT OUT THE DOOR
We define presidents as lame-duck when they no longer need to contend with elections, either presidential or midterm. For a one-term president who has lost a reelection bid, this period lasts just a few months, between their successor’s election and inauguration. For a second-term president, it can last two years, between the midterms and when they leave office. (Trump, who has never been particularly interested in the political fortunes of other Republicans, is unlikely to let the 2028 presidential election affect his thinking.)
Freed from the burdens of campaigning and legislating, and often lacking domestic political capital, lame-duck leaders tend to pivot to diplomacy, taking chances abroad that they would not have dared to before. Clinton tried to broker an Israeli-Palestinian peace agreement and arrange a presidential trip to North Korea at the end of his second term. After losing the 2014 midterms, President Barack Obama concluded the Iran nuclear deal and normalized relations with Cuba.
Lame-duck presidents have also used military force in ways they might not have done in the lead-up to elections. George H. W. Bush, for example, intervened in Somalia in late 1992 with a limited mission to ease the famine. More than a decade later, in 2007, George W. Bush sent a surge of forces to stabilize Iraq after a punishing midterm election in which voters seemed to send the message that he should withdraw from the failing war there.
The results of these foreign policy moonshots have been mixed. Clinton’s Israeli-Palestinian negotiations failed; Obama’s diplomatic wins were short-lived; George H. W. Bush’s Somalia mission was largely successful in staving off hunger but left the roots of the conflict unresolved, tempting Clinton to expand the mission with disastrous consequences; and George W. Bush’s Iraq surge quelled violence in the short term but did little to permanently stabilize the country. These endeavors were, at the very least, debated and planned with input from relevant parts of government and outside experts. Their aims were clear, even if unmet. And in each case the president attempted to explain and justify his policies—standards Trump has routinely failed to meet.
GOING FOR BROKE
With Trump now diminished by the midterms yet still on a quest to win a Nobel Peace Prize, one might expect him to turn to diplomacy. The problem is that he has already exhausted many of the obvious lame-duck gambits. During his first term, Trump swung for the foreign policy fences by pulling out of the 2015 Iran nuclear deal, meeting North Korean leader Kim Jong Un three times, replacing the North American Free Trade Agreement with his own regional trade pact, facilitating the normalization of ties between Israel and a handful of Arab countries, and withdrawing from a raft of international agreements. Since returning to office in 2025, he has presided over a cease-fire in Gaza and the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.
Trump is not expected to return to most of these initiatives because he has reached the limits of what his spectacle-driven diplomacy can achieve. Trump vowed to take Greenland, for example, but has settled for a deal that expands the U.S. military presence in the territory. His “Board of Peace,” which he pitched as a rival to the United Nations Security Council, will continue to languish as other countries now feel less need to kowtow to his every whim.
There are other long shots Trump could attempt, such as trying to end intractable conflicts in Kashmir or Sudan, to forge a reputation as a peacemaker. But these are exceptionally difficult problems to solve in the best of circumstances. Even forcing a lopsided deal in these cases would require a level of deftness, regional expertise, and patience that Trump lacks. He rarely invests meaningful time in diplomacy, as illustrated by his dubious claims to have ended a slew of conflicts, many of which are still ongoing.
Perhaps the biggest swing Trump could take would be to fashion a great-power concert—a forum in which he, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and Chinese leader Xi Jinping worked together to impose global order. As with most of his prior meetings with Putin and Xi, however, future summits are unlikely to produce anything of substance. Neither Russia nor China has expressed much interest in the trilateral nuclear arms treaty that Trump has floated. Nor are they keen on pressing Iran to acquiesce to a deal with the United States.
Trump could use those meetings to throw Ukraine or Taiwan under the bus in the desperate hope of a peace deal. But as the past two years have demonstrated, Putin is not interested in compromise and has the resources to keep fighting. Xi views Taiwan as a domestic Chinese matter and will be unlikely to accept any constraints on his approach to the island. Trump will eventually figure out that he’s better off capitalizing on the optics of a summit of the three leaders than putting in the work to reach any kind of agreement.
ONE FOR THE ROAD
Trump is most likely to take action in Iran. He seems to believe that escalating the war could break the stalemate and rescue his legacy. But Iranian leaders won’t back down in the face of more force. Instead, they will probably ramp up attacks on commercial shipping, strike Gulf allies, and ignore diplomatic overtures until Trump leaves office. Moreover, Trump’s own options may be limited: a more radical U.S. escalation against Iran, such as deploying troops to Kharg Island, would probably be so unpopular within his base that he would avoid it. Even Trump’s biggest supporters are growing tired of the high prices that his war has caused. Renewed conflict could plunge the world into economic crisis.
Trump could also attempt to force regime change in Cuba. He has imposed a full-blown embargo on the island for most of 2026 in an effort to weaken its defenses. Cut off from its Venezuelan lifeline and without electricity for all but a few hours a day, the economic hardships and human suffering in Cuba have dramatically worsened in recent months. Ousting Cuba’s government is a personal priority of Marco Rubio, Trump’s secretary of state and national security adviser, and would align with the “Donroe Doctrine,” an assertion of U.S. primacy in the Western Hemisphere.
For Trump, an attack on Cuba would be attractive because it would not require too much in the way of military assets and, at least in his mind, would solve a problem that has bedeviled U.S. presidents stretching back to the end of the Eisenhower administration. Trump might have already moved on Cuba had he not gotten bogged down in Iran. Of course, as the political scientist Alexander Downes has shown, using force to achieve regime change rarely works and often leads to unpredictable consequences—in the case of Cuba, it might mean a new influx of refugees to the United States.

But a lame-duck Trump could see it as a gamble worth taking on the off chance that he can be the president to finally unseat the communist regime. Israel’s election commission on Wednesday confirmed the final results of last week’s vote that stripped Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition of its governing majority, rejecting claims of mass fraud promoted by the prime minister.
The main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, said Netanyahu had launched a “pogrom against democracy” in attempting to hold on to power by discrediting valid votes and weaponising security forces against parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Hours earlier, Israel’s attorney general said she had blocked a demand from the Shin Bet security service to interrogate senior politicians from the Palestinian-led parties because she had not been presented with any evidence of wrongdoing.
“In a country governed by the rule of law, neither citizens nor elected officials can be interrogated without evidence that justifies doing so,” Gali Baharav-Miara said in a statement, after Haaretz reported on the attempt to target four politicians.
Election authorities on Wednesday presented the final results to the president, Isaac Herzog, after rejecting allegations they had been tainted by large-scale foreign interference and voter fraud.
“The review found no evidence of irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or affected its results,” the Central Elections Committee said in a statement.
The body’s chair, Noam Sohlberg, said some “suspicions” were still under investigation but “they do not cast doubt on the election as a whole or justify delaying the election results”.
When the results were handed over, Herzog denounced racist attacks on Palestinian citizens who had turned out to vote at historic rates.
“I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently,” he said. “I hold Arab society in Israel in great respect. I value its contribution to the country in every area of life, and its desire to integrate.”
Herzog will play a key role in the formation of the next government by choosing which politician has the first chance to create a coalition. He is expected to name Eisenkot, and the announcement could come as early as Thursday evening.
Late on Wednesday, the Palestinian grouping Ra’am said it would recommend that Eisenkot form the next government. The larger Palestinian grouping, Joint List, has said its priority is removing Netanyahu, so is expected to back Eisenkot as the strongest contender to achieve that.
A former leader of the Israeli military who lost his son fighting in Gaza, Eisenkot has secured the public support of all of the Jewish Israeli opposition parties.
However, negotiations could take weeks and Eisenkot warned of ongoing attempts to undermine trust in the election results. He accused Netanyahu of weaponising the security services against domestic opponents in an effort to hold on to power.
“The employees of the Ministry of Defense, law enforcement and the civil service in Israel are servants of the state, not the king,” he said in a statement. “Woe to anyone who abuses their authority and role for political considerations.”
The Shin Bet chief, David Zini, handpicked for the role by Netanyahu, had ordered the interrogations and sought to classify the investigation as a security file, which would have allowed harsher conditions including barring the politicians from having legal counsel.
Nadav Eyal, an Israeli journalist and commentator, said the public should brace for more extreme attempts to dismiss election results and discredit the leading opposition parties.
“The groundwork is steadily being laid for violence,” he wrote on X. “What you’re hearing breaking right now is the foundation of the legal and governmental orders in Israel.”
Netanyahu presided over a racist campaign targeting Palestinian citizens of Israel – about 20% of the population – and on election day began promoting the unfounded accusations of mass fraud now rejected by election authorities.
Ahmad Tibi, one of the most prominent and effective Palestinian politicians, was reportedly among those the Shin Bet sought to interrogate. He responded to the latest allegations, as news broke of sweeping victories for Democrats in the US midterms, with a swipe at Netanyahu’s fear of democracy.
“[The] attorney general is checking suspicion of ties between the Joint List and Democrats in the US,” Tibi wrote in a social media post. “According to the suspicion, in both cases the same sophisticated method was employed: people arrived in droves at the polling stations, cast a slip, and went home.”

President Donald Trump’s newly-renovated Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool was showing signs of cracking and peeling again - just hours after he declared the troubled project a success.
On Monday, Trump stood in front of the historic Washington, D.C., landmark to deliver a closing midterm election message and used the opportunity to celebrate the completion of a second round of renovations. He called the work “a complete job and we’re very proud of it.”
Shortly after his speech wrapped up, Washington Post reporters walking the perimeter of the reopened Reflecting Pool spotted several areas where the new coating appeared to be cracking or peeling.
The reporters also noted at least 20 other spots where the coating’s color was noticeably uneven, with light blue streaks appearing across the surface instead of the dark “American flag blue” Trump selected for the renovation.
“We fixed the leaks, we resurfaced the bottom in a beautiful dark blue,” Trump had said, adding that the pool had been finished with “the strongest coating you can get.”
A Department of the Interior spokesperson defended the project, crediting Trump with restoring the landmark and dismissing concerns about its appearance.
“The Reflecting Pool has never looked this beautiful and it's all thanks to President Donald J. Trump,” a spokesperson told The Independent. “He's an expert builder who was able to repair the pool in ways Obama and Biden could never even dream of.”
The spokesperson blamed the light-blue discoloration on “surplus coating,” saying the “lighter blue color will fade away or be lightly scrubbed off to show the beautiful American Flag Blue coating underneath.”
In a response to the Washington Post’s photos of the apparent cracks and peeling, the spokesperson said the damage was “stray pieces left over from the renovation and needed repairs due to deranged vandalism.”
“Those pieces will be picked up. Thanks to President Trump, the pool is clear, clean, leak-proof, and reflects the iconic scenery that surrounds this magical place,” the spokesperson added.
The cause of the latest issues is unclear. The National Park Service was reportedly aware of uneven coloring in areas that had already undergone a second round of repairs early last week, sources told the Post.
The latest problems come after the Reflecting Pool’s initial renovation quickly deteriorated earlier this year. Following the first round of repairs in the spring, the pool’s new lining began flaking shortly after it was refilled in June.
A Post investigation found that the pool’s lining deteriorated in at least 85 places, with an inspection report blaming the damage on renovation errors, including the use of improper materials and a rushed installation.
Coatings experts previously told the outlet that the materials used to line the pool require specific application techniques and drying times. Failure to follow those requirements can cause the coating to lose its adhesion.
The Trump administration initially blamed vandalism for the damage, leading to the arrest and prosecution of several people, including former Olympic athlete David Hearn.

articles.title: Death toll hits 40 after Russian strike on Ukrainian aid site; dozens remain missing - NBC News
articles.summary: Death toll hits 40 after Russian strike on Ukrainian aid site; dozens remain missing  NBC NewsUkraine says bodycam video shows deadly Russian double-tap bombing  BBCRussian bombing of Ukrainian aid center is one of the war’s ‘deadliest attacks,’ Zelensky says  CNNZelenskyy says 40 now confirmed dead after ‘insane’ Russian attack on school – as it happened  The GuardianDozens dead and missing after Russian strike on Ukrainian aid centre, officials say ...
articles.full_text:
The death toll from a Russian bombing of an aid distribution point in Ukraine’s southeastern Zaporizhzhia region on Monday has risen to 40, with dozens still missing, officials said, in one of the deadliest strikes on civilians this year.
The attack came a day after a brief U.S.-brokered local ceasefire expired and less than a week before the United States is due to bring together Ukrainian and Russian delegations in Abu Dhabi for talks on ending the war, now in its fifth year.
Reuters video on Wednesday showed men in military fatigues loading bodies in white plastic bags into the back of a van in the village of Komyshuvakha, which was struck multiple times.
Excavators were digging up earth near a huge blast crater while rescue workers searched underground for bodies.
Ivan Fedorov, the co-head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Defense Council, wrote on Telegram that 59 people were missing.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Russian forces first dropped aerial bombs on an underground school building being used as a distribution point as people arrived to collect aid, then struck the shelter with more bombs.
Classes have long since been suspended at the school because of its proximity to the front — Komyshuvakha lies some 11 miles from the nearest Russian positions — but it served as a shelter and handed out humanitarian aid every Monday, Zelenskyy said.
Two members of a rescue crew and four police officers were among the dead, emergency services said.
Russia’s defense ministry said the attack targeted Ukrainian military units around Komyshuvakha and two other settlements, and that up to 25 Ukrainian servicemen were killed.
Russia and Ukraine both deny deliberately targeting civilians.
Dramatic video
Bodycam video from one of the policemen killed in the attack, which Ukrainian police posted and Reuters verified, shows rubble and badly damaged buildings in the aftermath of the initial aerial attacks.
The policeman said the area was under threat from drones and appears to take shelter briefly inside the shell of a bombed-out building.
Later in the video, 15 to 20 people in civilian clothing are gathered outside the entrance to an underground shelter when a warning comes over a radio that Russian glide bombs are heading in the direction of the village.
Residents rush down several flights of stairs and toward a room, while the policeman with the bodycam turns through a door into what appears to be a temporary police station.
Three other men and a woman are visible in the final frames before there is a large explosion and the camera turns black.
In a social media post accompanying the video, the national police said several strikes hit the area, including from a 3-ton FAB bomb, which is a large bomb fitted with a glide kit that allows it to fly long distances after being dropped from a Russian warplane.
According to defense intelligence websites, a 3-ton glide bomb would carry around 1.4 tons of explosives.
Fighting resumes after brief local ceasefire
The strike occurred a day after a six-day ceasefire to evacuate civilians from the Russian-occupied southern Ukrainian town of Oleshky expired.
The truce, brokered by first lady Melania Trump, allowed nearly 800 people to be evacuated, according to the first lady. Zelenskyy awarded Trump a state honor for her role.
The United States will bring together delegations from Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10 and 11 to discuss ending the conflict, postwar security agreements and de-escalation, U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff said on Monday.

A bodycam video has been released by Ukraine police which they say shows the moments between two powerful Russian bomb strikes that killed at least 40 people at an aid centre and a shelter.
The footage, from a camera on one of the killed police officers, shows residents of the southern village of Kamyshuvakha going to an underground shelter after the first attack on Monday. Soon after a blast is heard and flames are seen as the shelter is hit.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said more than 30 people may still be under the rubble, as a search operation continued for the third day.
Nine gliding bombs, some weighing 3,000kg, hit the village as people had gathered to get humanitarian aid, Ukraine said.
The bodycam footage was released by Ukraine's national police on Wednesday.
It shows huge devastation after the first bomb strike on the village in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region, as shocked local residents stare at the rubble.
Severely damaged buildings are also seen.
A voice of a military official is then heard on a two-way radio warning police on the ground of more glide bombs being launched towards Kamyshuvakha.
"Quickly [go] to the shelter!" one of the police officers tells local residents, who are seen walking into the shelter - at least two floors underground.
Seconds later the shelter is hit, and the recording stops.
Ukraine said the shelter was near a local school, which was being used to distribute humanitarian aid.
BBC Verify has confirmed the video was filmed in the same place as footage released by the Ukrainian state emergencies service DSNS showing the aftermath Monday's attack in Komyshuvakha.
In a post on social media on Wednesday, Zelensky said that "nine aerial bombs were dropped by the Russians.
"First, they hit people who came to receive humanitarian aid, and then rescuers and police officers who arrived at the scene."
The Ukrainian president added that "unfortunately, there has been very little reaction from the world to this insane attack", describing it as yet another of "thousands" of war crimes committed by Russia.
Ukraine's DSNS earlier posted another video showing a huge crater left after the attack on Kamyshuvakha.
The Russian military has not publicly commented.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
In a separate development on Wednesday, Zelensky said he talked "in great detail for an hour-and-a-half" with US President Donald Trump's peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner ahead of trilateral negotiations between Ukraine, Russia and the US on 10-11 November in Abu-Dhabi.
The Ukrainian leader - who is currently making a surprise visit to Spain - also said his team had a separate "meaningful" meeting in Brussels with representatives from the US, the EU, France, Britain, Germany, as well as Nato and the World Bank about "post-war reconstruction".
He added that the meeting in Belgium's capital would continue on Thursday to discuss "security guarantees" for Ukraine.
Since the trilateral talks aimed at ending the war were suspended in February, Moscow has stepped up attacks as Kyiv virtually ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.
Analysts expect no major breakthrough when the talks resume in the capital of the United Arab Emirates.

articles.title: Russian attacks disrupt power in Kyiv, while the death toll in a stricken village rises to 40 - AP News

articles.full_text:
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russian attacks triggered power and water outages for hours Wednesday across Kyiv and surrounding regions while President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the death toll in a stricken village in southern Ukraine rose to 40 in one of the deadliest strikes there in nearly five years of war.
On Monday, multiple Russian guided bombs slammed into a former school and nearby shelter in the village of Komyshuvakha, near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region, as residents waited for humanitarian aid.
In addition to those killed, Zelenskyy said 30 more people could still be buried in the rubble.
“Unfortunately, there has been very little reaction from the world to this insane attack,” he said in a post on X. “But it, like thousands upon thousands of other war crimes Russia has committed against Ukraine and Ukrainians, demands a strong response. Evil always goes further if it is left unanswered.”
Elsewhere, Moscow showed no signs of letting up its aerial assaults.
Before water and power were restored, residents in the capital of Kyiv were urged to use public drinking water fountains. Emergency centers were set up hastily in the worst-hit areas, offering hot tea and power for people seeking to charge electrical devices.
Russia attacked overnight with 310 drones, including 81 jet-powered drones, according to Ukraine’s air force. In its daily social media report, the air force said it downed or suppressed 272 drones of various types.
Such attacks are a regular feature of wartime life in Ukraine despite arrest warrants issued by the International Criminal Court in 2024 for two senior Russian officers whom prosecutors accuse of overseeing strikes on civilian infrastructure.
EU talks focus on postwar support for Ukraine
Officials from the United States, Germany, France, Britain, NATO, the World Bank and the European Union met Wednesday at the European Commission’s headquarters in Brussels to discuss the massive reconstruction effort that will be required once the war ends.
The commission said in a brief statement after the closed-door meeting that it “focused on refining the scenarios for Ukraine’s postwar economic development and prosperity.”
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said she wanted the meeting to discuss European demands for Russian concessions in any negotiations. She said previous talks have been focused only on “what Ukraine should give away or what concessions they should make.”
The Brussels talks came ahead of a new round of U.S.-brokered peace negotiations next week, more than 4 1/2 years after Russia’s full-scale invasion of its neighbor.
Crews search for victims for a 3rd day in a southern village
Russian drones were hampering the search for victims in the village of Komyshuvakha, said Mykhailo Semikin, acting head of the regional military administration, but he added that operations there would continue.
Ivan Fedorov, co-chair of the regional defense council, said 12 bodies pulled from the rubble had been identified so far. The National Police of Ukraine said in a Telegram post that visual identification of some bodies was not possible and that specialists were working with relatives of the dead to collect DNA samples.
Body camera footage recovered from a police officer killed in the attack shows the devastating impact of the Russian guided bomb. The video was recorded Monday as the officer descended stairs into the shelter after the nearby aid distribution center was struck.
In the video, the officer speaks to survivors of the initial attack, urging them to seek shelter. “Go down! Why are you gathering here?” he is heard saying.
Moments after the officer enters a low-ceilinged underground room, a brief rumble is heard as the video cuts to black.
On Tuesday, Baptist pastor Vladyslav Makhovskyi joined the search for survivors. But as the day wore on, bodies wrapped in white plastic sheets were carried from the ruins and laid in rows as smoke drifted across the shattered landscape.
“When the bombs hit, people could no longer get out,” Makhovskyi told The Associated Press. “I understand that many were killed immediately. Even if some were still alive, they probably couldn’t breathe.”
First lady Melania Trump is honored by Ukraine
The attack followed the end of a six-day ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in the southwestern Ukrainian region of Kherson. It was the most significant truce between Kyiv and Moscow since 2022, and allowed the evacuation of residents from the shattered city.
Zelenskyy awarded U.S. first lady Melania Trump the Order of Princess Olga, 1st class — an honor for women who have made an outstanding contribution to the Ukrainian state.
She was recognized for her humanitarian support, including human rights and charitable activities aimed at helping Ukrainian children, according to the presidential website.
She was credited with brokering the ceasefire to allow those trapped in Oleshky to leave.
The Kremlin, meanwhile, expressed hope that U.S. President Donald Trump will continue his efforts to end the war in Ukraine regardless of the outcome of the midterm elections that saw Democrats take control of Congress, spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
Ukrainian probe uncovers more high-level corruption
The National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine said Wednesday it had uncovered a criminal plot involving senior officials from the country’s security service, prosecutor general’s office and national police who were alleged to have taken kickbacks from the criminal underworld in exchange for protecting fraudulent call centers, drug sales and illegal cigarette and currency operations.
It was the latest in a series of graft scandals that have plagued Zelenskyy’s presidency.
In September, former Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko resigned after investigators accused one of his subordinates of running a scheme linked to fraudulent call centers.
Moscow says it downs hundreds of Ukrainian drones
Meanwhile, Russia’s Ministry of Defense said that it shot down 709 Ukrainian drones overnight.
The major online retailer Ozon said that a drone attack caused a fire to break out at its logistics center in Adygeysk, in Russia’s Adygea region, but that there were no casualties.
___
Corder reported from The Hague, Netherlands. Associated Press writers Derek Gatopoulos in Kyiv, Elise Morton in London and Lorne Cook in Brussels contributed.

articles.title: Kyiv Independent hit by suspected Russian cyberattack - The Kyiv Independent
articles.summary: Kyiv Independent hit by suspected Russian cyberattack  The Kyiv IndependentHackers hit Ukraine and Russia's emergency apps, send fake nuclear alerts  ReutersFake warnings of nuclear attack posted on hacked Russian and Ukrainian emergency apps  CNNIn Kyiv, hackers sent fake alerts about a nuclear apocalypse. articles.full_text:
The Kyiv Independent came under a cyberattack on Nov. 4, resulting in website disruption and some readers receiving emails containing fake claims in Russian and English.
The content of the fake claims points to a Russian operation. Hackers gained access to the website’s content management system and to one of the services the Kyiv Independent uses to send newsletters.
“This is the first time an attack like this has happened to us, and we are treating it very seriously,” said Olga Rudenko, the Kyiv Independent’s editor-in-chief.
The attack has similarities with the hack of the government app that Ukrainians rely on for air raid alerts three days earlier.
The hackers sent four emails and posted similar messages on the website, which the Kyiv Independent staff deleted immediately.
The bank details of the Kyiv Independent’s members and donors are not at risk, as all payment and banking information is handled by secure third-party payment systems.
“Our team has been working on stopping this ugly attack since the night together with cybersecurity specialists. We are doing our best to identify all vulnerabilities and protect our platforms from possible future attacks,” says Zakhar Protsiuk, the Kyiv Independent’s chief operating officer.
“We are grateful for all the support and messages offering help that we received from our readers, members, and partners from different countries. This attack won’t stop us from doing our work.”
Emails that hackers sent contained fake claims about President Volodymyr Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The first email, sent at 1 a.m. Kyiv time on Nov. 4, claimed that “Zelensky launched a nuclear warhead at Kyiv” as “proof of friendship” after meeting with Putin, and contained a username of an anonymous Telegram channel. Telegram is a Russian messaging and social media app that is widely used in Ukraine. The channel had mocking messages and threats in Russian about attacking Ukrainians.
The email warned recipients in Russian to take shelter. Only a small minority of the Kyiv Independent’s audience live in Ukraine, with most readers based in English-speaking countries such as the U.S., the U.K., Canada, and Australia, as well as European countries.
A second Russian-language email was sent at 2:30 p.m. local time on Nov. 4. A similar email in English was sent at 3:05 p.m, followed by another email in Russian. The website simultaneously came under attack. These messages contained fake claims about a physical attack on Zelensky.
“Attacks like these are part of the war we cover every day — an attempt to sow confusion and erode trust,” Rudenko said.
The attack against the Kyiv Independent comes days after Ukraine's air raid alert app was hacked. Several fake alerts were sent to users’ phones, warning of nuclear, chemical, and street fighting threats, as well as a fake message in Russian.
"Hi! A nuclear alert is about to go off all across Ukraine! Don't worry, the Oreshnik (missile) is on its way," one of the false warnings read in Russian on the air alert app, which was developed in collaboration between the Digital Transformation Ministry and security technology company Ajax Systems.
The false alerts were then cleared about an hour later. President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the hack was a Russian attack in an interview with PBS News on Nov. 2.
“It was a cyberattack, one of the hundreds and thousands of those made by Russians before on banking systems, on pensions, social support, a lot of different support for civilians.”
“Of course, they want each day to make chaos in Ukraine, in all our cities. It's one of such steps by Russia,” he said.
For media inquiries: press@kyivindependent.com

Ahmad Bakhshayesh Ardestani, a member of Iranian parliament’s security committee, said Iran would fire on any European base used against it, including in Italy and Germany. State-run media said any new confrontation could reach “the heart of Europe".
Iranian lawmakers have threatened missile strikes on European countries hosting US military bases, as state-run media warned on Wednesday that any renewed confrontation with the US could reach "the heart of Europe".
"If America uses its bases in Europe, including in Italy and Germany, Iran's missiles will be fired towards Europe," Ahmad Bakhshayesh Ardestani, a member of parliament's National Security Committee, told Euronews.
"In the two previous wars we did not do this, but this time we will not let Europe's assistance to America for an attack on Iran go without consequence;" Ardestani added.
Asked whether Europe was entering a new phase of war with Iran, Ardestani said European countries had already been at war with Iran in the previous phase by allowing their bases to be used.
He said Iran would strike any base used against it and would also target "the material and non-material assets of countries that assist America."
A second committee member, Fada Hossein Maleki, said Iran had prepared a new approach and scenario for any renewed conflict that he believed would surprise both the US and European countries.
German embassy message
The IRGC issued a statement on Wednesday — the anniversary of the 1979 seizure of the US embassy in Tehran, marked in Iran as "the day of fighting global arrogance" — pledging "an immediate, effective response without geographical limits to every level and type of threat."
The statement cited orders attributed to Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei calling for updating Iran's "target bank" and placing "the enemy's material and non-material assets within range."
Ahead of Wednesday's anniversary marches, government supporters hung a banner outside the German embassy in Tehran carrying a quote from the secretary of Iran's National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, "Europe will pay the price for supporting Israel."
IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency identified those responsible as members of the student Basij at the University of Tehran.
Euronews sought comment from the German embassy in Tehran and Germany's foreign ministry on whether the banner had been placed on the embassy railings. Both were unreachable at the time of publication.
Fars reported separately that Iran had warned Germany its military assets across the region would be treated as "legitimate defensive targets" if Berlin entered open military confrontation with Iran. The claim could not be independently verified.
Tehran has summoned Germany's ambassador in recent weeks over Berlin's support for Israel.
Kayhan newspaper, published under the supervision of a representative of Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, wrote that Iran's range of potential targets was no longer confined to US bases in the Middle East and could extend to "the heart of Europe," citing an order attributed to Khamenei for a "military response without geographical limits."
Rezaei wrote on X that the US response to Iran's demands had been "not convincing," saying Washington would need to meet Iran's seven conditions in full before reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
Parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf welcomed the Republicans' defeat in Tuesday's congressional elections in a post on X, writing that the American people had "said no to war" and that Iran supported that message.
"If the US government ignores the public will in order to act in favour of managers who pay bribes and engage in international blackmail, it will realise that our 'no' comes with a nightmare," Ghalibaf added.
Asked whether he planned to take a tougher line against Iran, US President Donald Trump gave an ambiguous answer, saying he would examine the matter and act if needed.

Iran has called the US response to its seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz “unconvincing” as US President Donald Trump confirmed launching strikes on an Iranian island near the strategic waterway.
The developments on Tuesday came as Qatar stepped up diplomatic efforts to avert a renewed war between the US and Iran and as another oil tanker was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz.
The indirect talks centre on an Iranian proposal to reopen the waterway over two days, if the US meets Tehran’s seven demands, including the lifting of sanctions and ending a US naval blockade.
Despite reports of progress in recent days, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said on Tuesday that Washington’s response had fallen short.
“America’s response to Iran’s rights and demands was not convincing, and they must fully and explicitly address Iran’s seven conditions and act upon them,” he wrote on X.
“Only in this case will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened.”
His post came after Majed al-Ansari, a spokesperson for Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said that talks were continuing and that both sides “remain committed to the negotiation process“.
He said Qatar was facilitating the “real-time exchange of proposals between” the US and Iran.
Attack on Qeshm Island
In Washington, DC, Trump confirmed the US had struck Iran early on Tuesday, telling Fox News that the strikes had targeted an anti-aircraft facility.
He described the operation as a “minor attack” and said it “wasn’t war”.
“They built an anti-aircraft facility. It took them about two months. We watched it get built. As soon as it was completed, we hit it last night,” he said.
Iranian media said the strikes hit Qeshm Island in the Gulf near the Strait of Hormuz. Earlier in the day, US officials told US media that the strikes had been “defensive” and followed Iranian fire at an American aircraft.
The strikes came as US media, citing US officials, reported that Central Command had prepared plans for strikes that could begin as early as Wednesday, after the midterm elections, when three American aircraft carriers would be in the region.
The crucial elections could cost Trump’s Republicans control of both the House and the Senate, and fears have grown that Trump could carry out a threatened attack on Iran once the vote is over.
US media have previously reported that the planned campaign would be short and intense.
Trump meanwhile repeated warnings of further military action on Tuesday, saying, “I’m not looking to … kill lots of people” and “If we have to, we’ll have to.”
In an earlier interview with the Financial Times, he suggested he was content with the state of the stand-off with Iran. “We seem to be getting everything we want,” the paper quoted him as saying in a six-minute telephone interview.
Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, meanwhile ordered the military at the weekend to respond to any threat immediately and without geographical limits, and to update its list of targets.
Iranian officials have suggested that European countries and undersea cables in the Gulf could be targeted.
Tanker struck in Hormuz
As officials weighed the possibility of escalation, commercial shipping came under further attack.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed on Wednesday that four oil tankers were destroyed after striking naval mines while attempting to pass through a prohibited shipping lane south of the Strait of Hormuz.
The tankers remained ablaze following the explosions, the IRGC said in a statement carried by the official IRNA news agency. Two other vessels were detained for violating shipping restrictions, it added.
Earlier, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported that two unidentified projectiles struck a tanker’s engine room about 14 nautical miles (26km) northeast of Oman’s coastal village of Limah on Tuesday. No casualties were reported.
It could not be independently verified whether the incidents reported by UKMTO and the IRGC were linked.
The IRGC also claimed its air defence forces shot down a US-made MQ-9 drone over the strait at 4.30am local time (01:00GMT), describing it as the 56th such aircraft it had downed.
The statement said the operations were carried out by the IRGC’s naval and aerospace forces, which had inflicted “heavy blows on the enemy”.
John Mearsheimer, a US political scientist, questioned whether another short bombing campaign could achieve Washington’s objectives, warning that Iranian retaliation could draw the US into a longer confrontation.
“If the 40-day bombing campaign didn’t work, how is the three-day bombing campaign going to work?” he asked in a video commentary, referring to the initial US-Israeli air campaign and proposals for a shorter renewed offensive.
He argued that an Iranian response could prompt further US escalation, increasing the damage to the global economy.

articles.title: Brazil publishes first global ‘roadmap’ for phasing out fossil fuels - The Guardian
articles.summary: Brazil publishes first global ‘roadmap’ for phasing out fossil fuels  The GuardianBrazil wraps up COP30 with fossil fuel, forest roadmaps, urging shift from talks to action  ReutersCOP30 Presidency Roadmap  COP30 Brasil AmazôniaBrazil puts forward a plan to wean the world off fossil fuels  Los Angeles TimesRoadmaps for Transitioning Away From Fossil Fuels  International Institute for Sustainable Development
articles.full_text:
All countries can start to break their dependence on fossil fuels now without needing to wait for new technologies or economic changes, Brazil’s government has said ahead of a global climate summit.
Brazil, the host of last year’s UN climate conference, set out the world’s first global “roadmap” for phasing out fossil fuels on Tuesday, showing that countries could boost their economies and pull people out of poverty while breaking the link with coal, oil and gas.
But Joeri Rogelj, a professor of climate science and policy at Imperial College London, said that although the Brazilian roadmaps represented a step forward, they were limited. “The roadmaps are valuable but fall short of clearly indicating the pace of change needed by including no timeline or key benchmarks,” he said.
“Because of this omission, they still leave much to be imagined about what is needed to achieve the Paris agreement’s ultimate goal: limiting global warming to well below 2C, and preferably to 1.5C, to avoid dangerous climate harm.”
André Corrêa do Lago, Brazil’s president of the Cop30 summit, said the roadmaps were intended to help move the annual UN Cops away from their previous focus on negotiating global agreements to tackle the climate crisis, and on to implementing the targets that had already been agreed. Cop31 takes place in Antalya, Turkey, this month.
“They are documents of implementation,” Corrêa do Lago told the Guardian in an interview. “There is a different group of people that negotiate and that implement. The problem we’ve had at many Cops is to think that the same people who negotiate might also need to coordinate the implementation – this is not the case.”
He said the roadmaps should be taken up by ministries of finance, transportation, energy and infrastructure to work on how they could be implemented in each country.
Brazil hosted the Cop30 summit last November in the coastal city of Belém, in the Amazon rainforest, where a bitter dispute broke out over whether the final set of resolutions should include pledges on fossil fuels. As a compromise, the presidency agreed to produce two roadmaps, one on “transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems in a just orderly and equitable manner” and the other on halting and reversing deforestation.
These roadmaps are separate from similarly named plans from governments that met after Cop30 at a conference in Santa Marta, Colombia, in April, to discuss the transition away from fossil fuels. At that conference, nearly 60 countries formed a new “coalition of the willing”, separate to Cops, to set out their own national roadmaps to phase out fossil fuels. Several countries have since produced national plans, including Germany, France and the Netherlands.
The roadmaps produced by governments under the Santa Marta initiative are much more specific and prescriptive than Brazil’s, as each of those is written by the national government responsible for implementing the policies recommended.
The Brazilian roadmaps only set out steps that are possible. They are not binding, they contain no deadlines or milestones for actions, and they leave it to countries themselves to “diagnose” their degree of dependence on fossil fuels and select steps to reduce it.
“Every country will have a different rhythm [for moving away from fossil fuels] – it’s very important to concentrate on the diagnoses of countries’ circumstances,” Corrêa do Lago said. “Based on these diagnoses, they can choose their levers [of policy] and implement the transition.”
Among the steps Brazil suggests is for oil and gas producers to urgently cut the flaring and venting of gas from extraction sites. Methane is a greenhouse gas 80 times more powerful than carbon dioxide, so this would have an immediate impact. Other steps are for countries to reduce their subsidies to fossil fuel use or production, and building up renewable generation.
The roadmap on deforestation notes the large sums that are expected to be needed to help poor countries with heavily forested areas such as the Amazon, the Congo rainforests and south-east Asian tropical forests that are under threat from fires and palm oil exploitation.
About $300bn is likely to be needed every year for forests by 2030, and $500bn a year by 2050, according to the roadmap, citing UN figures. The current amounts available fall far short at about $85bn a year.
At Cop30 last year, Brazil set up the Tropical Forest Forever Facility, a fund aiming to preserve forests, which raised about $7bn from various countries including a £400m loan from the UK.
The deforestation roadmap also notes the importance of regulating trade between forested countries and consumer countries. At present, there are few trade checks to stop unscrupulous companies from selling goods from deforested areas.
In some cases, deforestation has appeared to be condoned or encouraged by local or even national administrations. Indonesia is being sued by civil society groups for “gross negligence” over the record-breaking fires over the last few months that have cleared swathes of forest and destroyed wildlife habitats, most likely to be replaced by palm oil plantations.
Brazil was able to publish the roadmaps after its president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, won a fourth election term just over a week ago. In the last four years under Lula, deforestation rates have fallen by about 70%. His defeated opponent Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the jailed ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, had been expected if elected to return to his father’s policies of rampant exploitation of the Amazon rainforest.

articles.title: Trump’s troubles with Iran could open the door to China - The Guardian
articles.summary: Trump’s troubles with Iran could open the door to China  The GuardianChina Won’t Bail Out Trump’s Lost War  Foreign PolicyBeijing launches diplomatic flurry amid threat of renewed U.S. war with Iran  The Washington PostChina's Wang urges Middle East dialogue in meetings with Iranian, Saudi officials  ReutersIran looks to China and Russia for leverage in US talks  Iran International
articles.full_text:
China has held a flurry of meetings with Gulf leaders in a sign that Beijing is stepping up its diplomatic efforts in the Middle East.
The diplomatic salvo comes before a highly anticipated meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping when the US president is expected to attend the Apec conference in Shenzhen, China, on 18 and 19 November.
Xi held talks with Haitham bin Tariq, Oman’s sultan, in a historic state visit to Beijing on Monday.
President Xi’s foreign minister, Wang Yi, met Saudi Arabia’s national security adviser, Musaad bin Mohammed Al Aiban, and the deputy secretary of Iran’s national security council, Ali Bagheri Kani.
Haitham’s trip to Beijing is the first time that an Omani head of state has visited China since the two countries established diplomatic relations nearly 50 years ago. According to a Chinese readout of the meeting, Xi warned that the Middle East should not become an arena for “great power rivalry and geopolitical conflicts”.
He said: “China has always been actively committed to stopping conflict and promoting peace, and hopes to contribute wisdom and solutions to resolving the regional security dilemma.”
Wang said after his separate talks that China was willing to “play a constructive role in helping the region emerge from the shadow of the pandemic and achieve lasting peace and stability”. In his meeting with Bagheri Kani, Wang said China supported Iran “in safeguarding its sovereignty and security”. According to China, the Iranian official said his country looked forward to China “playing a more important role in international and regional peace”.
When the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February, China was credited with pushing Tehran toward ceasefire talks in Pakistan, bolstering its status as a regional mediator.
Beijing’s influence in the Middle East is “no longer what it used to be”, said Shen Dingli, a Shanghai-based scholar of international relations. But he added: “Given China’s increased investment and trade in the region … its influence cannot be ignored.”
As the war has dragged on, China’s diplomatic efforts have been muted. Its biggest economic leverage over Iran is the fact that it buys about 90% of the Middle Eastern country’s crude oil exports. Between April and June, it slashed its crude imports by 30%, with the total in June plunging to the lowest level in a decade. That saved the global economy from a major spike in inflation. According to some estimates, China’s cut in oil imports shaved $30 or more off barrel prices of Brent crude, a global benchmark.
Beijing has otherwise done little to broker peace in the Middle East. That is partly because it does not see the conflict as being its responsibility to resolve. In March, Wang said the war “should never have happened” and that the US and Israel would find “no popular support” for the strikes.
China is also a beneficiary from the damage that the fighting has done to the US’s global reputation.
According to findings published in July by the Pew Research Center, a Washington-based thinktank, China is now viewed more favourably than the US in a majority of 36 countries surveyed.
The pain caused by the long-term disruption to the strait of Hormuz, the waterway through which much of the world’s oil and gas flows, also poses a risk to China’s economy. Shortages of energy cause inflation, which risks reducing global demand for Chinese goods.
Tehran and Washington are locked in intensive talks to reach an agreement, which could include reopening the strait. Trump has repeatedly threatened to renew military action against Iran after Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US, a move which would cause alarm in Beijing.
Trump’s desperation to reach a deal in the Middle East may also provide an opportunity for China to present itself as a regional peacemaker, bolstering Xi’s status before their meeting. Beijing brokered a detente between Saudi Arabia and Iran in 2023 but since then its diplomatic impact in the region has been limited.
Shen said China’s desire to improve diplomatic relations with Middle Eastern countries as well as the US were “mutually reinforcing” trends.
China’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Mao Ning, said on Monday that China would send special envoy Zhai Jun to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia in early to mid-November.

MotoGP is due to begin practice in Qatar in three days, but in the meantime the US has attacked an Iranian island.
The Qatar MotoGP is due to run this weekend on 5–8 November. Five of the six manufacturers are due to take part, with only Yamaha having confirmed it will not race in Lusail in a statement issued after last weekend’s Malaysian Grand Prix.
The race has been in some degree of uncertainty ever since the US-Israeli war on Iran began in February. At first, the Qatar race was postponed from its original April date until November, and by now the instability in the Middle East has led to concern from people in the paddock, most notably some of the riders, about racing at Lusail.
So far only the aforementioned Yamaha has decided to skip the Qatar round, with MotoGP making its displeasure at that decision public with its own statement on Sunday.
With the rest of the paddock travelling to Qatar this week, it will do so after reports last week suggested that the US and Israel were preparing to renew their offensive against Iran.
And the travel now comes amid reports last night (2 November) of a US attack against the Iranian island Qeshm, which sits in the Strait of Hormuz and has been used to attack shipping vessels in the waterway that has become synonymous with the conflict.
Reuters and the Associated Press have reported that last night’s attack was against Iranian surface-to-air missile capabilities on Qeshm.

articles.title: NATO’s New Defense Plan Includes Strikes Deep Into Russia - Kyiv Post
articles.summary: NATO’s New Defense Plan Includes Strikes Deep Into Russia  Kyiv PostNATO’s New Defense Plan Would Mean Strikes Deep Inside Russia  WSJNATO prepares new defence plan foreseeing strikes deep inside Russian territory – WSJ  Українська правдаIs NATO preparing a preemptive strike against Belarus? Fact-checking News.by claims  Беларускі расследавальніцкі цэнтрNATO considers conventional strategic strikes in Russia if a member is attacked  Meta-Defense
articles.full_text:
NATO is developing defense plans that envision strikes deep inside Russia if Moscow attacks alliance territory, targeting the bases, supply networks, and industrial facilities supporting an invasion.
The approach, developed under NATO’s supreme allied commander in Europe, U.S. Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, reflects lessons from Russia’s war against Ukraine: Stopping advancing troops requires disrupting the military system behind them, according to The Wall Street Journal.
For decades, European defense planning focused on preventing Soviet or Russian forces from advancing after crossing NATO borders. Alliance strategists now consider that approach insufficient.
Polish Maj. Gen. Ireneusz Nowak told the Journal that defense also requires the ability to strike back.
In the event of a conflict with Russia, we would certainly want to strike its military-industrial base, he said, describing precision strikes deep inside Russian territory as a means of deterrence.
Nowak argued that if Ukraine had possessed that capability at the outset of the invasion, the war would not have developed into positional fighting resembling World War I.
The plans envision attacks roughly 150 kilometers (93 miles) to thousands of kilometers behind the front line, using precision missiles and less expensive weapons such as drones, the Journal reported.
Potential targets extend beyond airfields and military bases to industrial facilities, critical infrastructure, and raw material resources supporting Russia’s war effort. The aim is to make such strikes an automatic component of NATO’s response to a Russian attack.
Grynkewich outlined the approach at a recent security conference in Warsaw as part of what he called his “theory of victory.”
NATO forces would first stop the opening wave of an attack, then undermine the enemy’s ability to sustain subsequent operations. If the offensive continued, the alliance would strike both attacking forces and the networks supplying, supporting, and directing them.
The strategy does not envision escalation to nuclear weapons. NATO also held its first symposium devoted to deep strikes in June.
Precision weapons are central to the approach, including established systems such as Tomahawk cruise missiles and ATACMS ballistic missiles, alongside weapons still under development.
European countries are seeking to expand stocks of Storm Shadow, SCALP, and Taurus cruise missiles while developing additional systems.
Fabian Hoffmann, a senior research fellow at the Norwegian Institute for Defense Studies, told the newspaper that 20 European manufacturers were pursuing at least 48 projects to develop inexpensive cruise missiles, though not all would succeed.
Ukraine has increasingly pursued a similar approach, striking military and economic targets inside Russia with longer-range weapons, including domestically developed Flamingo cruise missiles, according to the report.
Analysts cautioned that military planning alone would not guarantee political approval to carry out the strikes.
Nico Lange, a former senior German Defense Ministry official, told the Journal that a gap remained between military plans incorporating offensive action to defend against Russia and political views that equate defense primarily with barriers or a “drone wall.”
The unresolved question, according to the report, is whether European leaders would authorize the operations their military planners consider necessary to stop and defeat an attack.

articles.title: Chris Mason: The US elections will change Trump – how will Burnham react? - BBC
articles.summary: Chris Mason: The US elections will change Trump – how will Burnham react?  BBCSee more headlines & perspectives on Google News
articles.full_text:
The first public words from the prime minister after the American midterm elections were instantly revealing about contemporary international politics and diplomacy.
"Well, President Trump has accepted the results," Andy Burnham said.
It is not an observation British leaders have frequently had to make about recent American presidents - that they are not disputing the result of elections in their own country. But what would previously have been taken for granted no longer can be.
Burnham remains in the foothills of establishing a relationship with the president – so far it has amounted to a handful of phone calls and one face-to-face meeting at the United Nations in New York in September.
As he continues to attempt to build a rapport with Donald Trump, he will be doing so with a president in a wildly different political situation than when Sir Keir Starmer was trying to build bridges with him.
No longer is this a story of an extraordinary comeback, but of a midterm president seemingly punished for the consequences of a foreign war the type of which he had originally promised to avoid.
And it is noticeable that the British government's public reaction is grounded too in the consequences of the war with Iran: the cost of living.
"I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all and that's the cost of living," the prime minister said.
"But I can't get people's cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, the conflict in Ukraine started by Russia."
Within government the Iran war and its consequences, particularly on energy prices, is widely seen as the biggest individual contributor among the many factors currently driving up the cost of living.
And, bluntly, it is one that puts many, including many of America's allies, in alignment with many in America, Democrat and Republican, who when asked why these elections went as they did, point at the prices displayed outside any petrol station.
Speaking before the votes in America were counted, the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband reflected on this when I spoke to him on BBC Newscast.
When I asked him specifically if he feared that a domestically humiliated Trump may prove more belligerent internationally, it was to the Iran war the foreign secretary referred.
He didn't offer a direct answer to my question, but chose instead to say this: "I know that one of the biggest responsibilities of the whole government, frankly, is the cost of living situation at home, and we know one of the biggest contributors to the cost of living situation is, frankly, the conflict."
"The Strait of Hormuz being not exactly closed, but not properly open, not free-flowing, and that is hitting families at home," he said.
"We know that we need a diplomatic way out of this conflict, and so that is one of the things that we're working on. It's something I talked to the US Secretary of State about at the G20, and it's something we continue to work on," he added.
The foreign secretary met Marco Rubio at the meeting in Atlanta last week.
But the big question for the British government, and so many others, is does defeat at home make it more likely that President Trump gets angrier abroad?
Or, do America's traditional allies, the UK, the European Union, Canada, Australia and others feel more strident and willing to work with Donald Trump's domestic political opponents to try to challenge and restrain a weakened president?
The answers to these two final questions will determine much in world affairs in the next couple of years.

The strategy calls not only for stopping an offensive but also for striking military facilities and industry deep behind the front lines inside Russia.
NATO is reviewing ways to counter possible Russian aggression and developing a defense strategy that would abandon previous restrictions and carry out conventional strikes deep inside Russian territory.
This is reported by The Wall Street Journal.
Experience from the war in Ukraine and conflicts in the Middle East is prompting military commanders to rethink how to counter the Russian army. For decades, NATO’s eastern flank defenses relied on barriers and checkpoints. But after nearly five years of war in Ukraine, Alliance strategists have concluded that obstacles alone cannot stop a possible Russian invasion.
Deterring the Kremlin’s conventional armed forces now requires more active prevention, or, in military terms, denial. This means not only destroying troops that could pour across the border, but also striking military bases, supply depots and industrial facilities deep behind the front lines, on Russian territory itself.
NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe Alexus Grynkewich set out this approach in his “theory of victory.” Under it, allies would first stop the initial wave of an attack and then deprive the adversary of the ability to continue its offensive.
We will dismantle the system of warfare deployed against us by striking both the forces advancing and everything that supports, supplies or controls those forces
– Alexus Grynkewich
The plan as presented does not envisage resorting to nuclear weapons, The Wall Street Journal notes.
Polish Major General Ireneusz Nowak called the main lesson of Ukrainian resistance the need to respond to aggression with force. In his words, “defense also means striking back.”
In the event of an armed confrontation with Russia, we would certainly want to strike its defense industry. We must treat precision strikes deep behind the front lines as a tool of deterrence
– Ireneusz Nowak
Nowak added that the Alliance’s shared message to Moscow should be clear:
Don’t do anything foolish, because we can punish you. But to be credible, we need to have these capabilities
– Ireneusz Nowak
The strategy effectively echoes the principle of “hitting the archer instead of defending against the arrows,” which Ukraine applies by using long-range drones and missiles to attack Russian oil refineries, factories producing batteries for drones, data centers and fuel depots.
Ukraine’s ambassador to NATO, Aliona Hetmanchuk, also stressed the importance of long-range impact at a conference on the subject. She compared air defense to painkillers that “may relieve the symptoms, but you need to eliminate the source of the pain itself.”
To implement this doctrine, the United States is modernizing and replenishing its stocks of long-range Tomahawk cruise missiles and ATACMS ballistic missiles. European partners aim to increase stocks of Storm Shadow, SCALP and Taurus cruise missiles, while also developing new, low-cost long-range weapons.
Fabian Hoffmann, a senior researcher at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, noted that at least 48 projects to develop low-cost cruise missiles had been announced in Europe.
What we have seen proves that you would not want to find yourself in a high-intensity conflict where your adversary has access to powerful long-range strike arsenals and you do not
– Fabian Hoffmann

articles.title: Left-wing Democrat Abdul El-Sayed wins in Michigan to become first Muslim senator - BBC
articles.summary: Left-wing Democrat Abdul El-Sayed wins in Michigan to become first Muslim senator  BBCPolitics of fear failed to stop El-Sayed's historic US Senate win  ReutersGiddy Democrats let the mask slip with DEI boasts and Arabic taunts  The TelegraphAbdul El-Sayed’s Senate Win Is Big to Muslim Americans, but Not Because of Faith  The New York TimesAbdul El-Sayed welcomes Trump's plan to cut Israel aid, calls for end to arms sales  NPR
articles.full_text:
Left-wing Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has won in the battleground state of Michigan to become the US's first Muslim senator, following a race fuelled by withering attacks and inter-party disputes.
El-Sayed bested Republican Mike Rogers, withstanding an onslaught of attacks that included baselessly tying him to terrorism and a high-profile spat with a fellow Democrat.
Rogers, backed by President Donald Trump, portrayed El-Sayed as a communist, criticising his stance on Israel and his Muslim faith.
After waiting long hours, watching the wave of Democratic gains across the country, El-Sayed's supporters celebrated wildly when he took the stage to mark his victory.
The former public health administrator campaigned on a left-wing platform that included universal health care and a wealth tax on billionaires.
The win comes days after El-Sayed's Democratic primary rival, Haley Stevens, endorsed Rogers, the Republican candidate, just days before the election.
El-Sayed's supporters gave deafening cheers when he took to the stage, as they chanted his name in jubilation. A sea of iPhones were held up to take in this moment of history - a Muslim man elected to the Senate.
Several people in the crowd embraced, filled with emotion. They repeated his slogan back to him like they were at a concert: "Money out of politics, money in your pocket and Medicare for all."
On the campaign trail, El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, described Israel's actions in Gaza as genocide and called for an end to US aid to the country.
The issue carries particular resonance in Michigan, which is home to the second largest Arab-American population in the US.
It also fuelled tensions between El-Sayed and Stevens, a staunch supporter of Israel, whose primary campaign received millions of dollars in backing from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac).
The contest was widely seen as a test of the political influence of the Democratic left in a key battleground state, following a series of primary wins by democratic socialist candidates in more politically favoured districts.
El-Sayed thanked the crowd in the early hours of Wednesday morning for taking a chance on "the unlikeliest of candidates" and rounded on his opponents.
"They went all in on one of the ugliest campaigns we've seen in a long time," he said, accusing them of attacking him "because of my name and my faith".
"They wanted an America that is too small for some of us. We know that this is an America that is big enough for all of us," El-Sayed added.
Supporters 'proud' of win
This is a milestone for Muslim Americans who had to watch, along with their children, as El-Sayed was attacked with increasing anti-Muslim rhetoric, including directly from the president of the United States. It comes at a time of rising in Islamophobia nationwide.
Roula Allouch, an Arab American Muslim, told the BBC she had goosebumps from the success of the campaign.
"I'm proud of Abdul, the campaign that he ran, his family for their perseverance through all the hate, the Islamophobic rhetoric that was thrown at him throughout this campaign," she said.
Another Muslim woman in the crowd was equally moved and told the BBC his win meant everything to her.
"He makes us so proud and it just makes us feel like we can stand a little taller, broaden our shoulders and know somebody has our back and that he's going to be in Washington really fighting for us," she said.
El-Sayed has certainly shown on the campaign trail that he's willing to hit back at Maga attacks. In his victory speech, he used the Arabic phrase "Alhamdullah", and then trolled Republicans by saying that "for the rightwing ops, that just means praise be to God".
El-Sayed, 42, represents a generation of Arab Americans and Muslims who were born in the United States to immigrant parents and grew up in post-9/11 America.
Celebrating with family from Chicago, another South Asian Muslim supporter of El-Sayed's said the moment was historic for everyone who has been made to feel that they don't belong in America or have a place in politics.
"If someone with the name of Abdul can make it, that means this next generation can look up and say that they can too," she told the BBC.
'One of the tightest races'
The Michigan Senate seat, previously held by retiring Democrat Gary Peters, was considered by analysts to be one of the tightest races in Tuesday's midterm elections.
El-Sayed's win further cements Democrats' control of the US Senate after a wave of wins - including in deep-Republican areas.
He had to contend with massive outside spending heavily favouring Rogers and his opponent in the Democratic primary, Haley Stevens. He's been unapologetic and unwavering in his stances.
In presidential elections, Michigan is one of the crucial swing states - the state voted for Joe Biden in 2020 but Donald Trump in 2024.
Many had questioned whether Stevens' last-minute endorsement of Rogers would make a difference in the race.
Democratic leadership called it "a despicable betrayal" and her staff reportedly resigned in mass. Voters who spoke with the BBC in the state said they were confused over the move, with some questioning whether the congresswoman was acting out of anger.
El-Sayed attempted to ignore the dramatic turn, telling reporters that he doesn't "think about Haley Stevens" and "none of this matters".
Throughout his campaign, El-Sayed has channelled grassroots frustration with Washington politics as well as US ties to Israel. He took on money in politics and argued against Trump's policies, which he blamed for raising costs for voters in the state.
He campaigned with left-wing leaders Sen Bernie Sanders and Rep Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
