articles.title: NPT 2.0: Updating the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Regime - Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas
articles.summary: NPT 2.0: Updating the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Regime  Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas
articles.full_text:
By Arjun Goswami and Svyambhuv Talwar
Summary: Drawing on nearly a century of non-proliferation regime and regional conflicts, this blog explores whether the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) remains effective in today’s geopolitical environment. The NPT’s current framework appears to exacerbate, rather than mitigate, the risks of nuclear and conventional conflict. Accordingly, it may be appropriate to consider a “NPT 2.0” framework based on revised admission criteria for nuclear-weapon states, reciprocal obligations for the P5, and a clearly defined withdrawal mechanism. This blog also explores how India could help shape this new global bargain.
Introduction
Access to nuclear weapons tends to be a deeply polarised debate. Advocates of nuclear non-proliferation argue that the horrors of Hiroshima and Nagasaki should never be repeated, while critics believe that nuclear weapons were used in a singular moment on the back of untold Japanese atrocities against other populations and in the face of war weariness by the Allies confronted with determined kamikaze type resistance by the Japanese armed forces. Non-nuclear weapon states argue that the resulting nuclear non-proliferation regime is one based on hypocrisy and nuclear apartheid, where existing nuclear weapons states are granted access to such weapons and others are not.
As the world faces the consequences of a Middle Eastern conflict, largely connected to concerns about Iran’s access to nuclear weapons, it may be prudent to examine objectively how the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) was established. Comparing different regional conflicts may also help determine whether the NPT needs to be updated.
History of nuclear non-proliferation law
To understand the issue of access to nuclear weapons, knowledge of the history of international law governing nuclear non-proliferation is a must. To accelerate the end of the war against Japan, the United States developed and then exploded nuclear bombs in Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945. However, its attempts at keeping the nuclear weapons technology a secret and solely in the hands of the United States failed. With the help of Communist spies, the Soviet Union gained access to nuclear weapons by 1949. The United Kingdom gained access to nuclear weapons by 1952, followed by France in 1960, and China in 1964. Thus, the five permanent members of the UN Security Council, the so called P5, had all acquired nuclear weapons by 1964.
As nuclear arms proliferation started to spread, US President Dwight Eisenhower gave a speech at the UN General Assembly in 1953, advocating a so-called “Atoms for Peace” programme, which was designed to launch the use of nuclear equipment and research for various peaceful means rather than warfare. The underpinning of this speech was to win the hearts and minds of developing countries towards the peaceful use of nuclear research, such as nuclear power or nuclear medicine, and confine nuclear arms access to a limited number of countries.
These initial efforts to limit access to nuclear arms were further promoted through the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). Launched in 1957 with an American, Sterling Cole, as its first Director General, the IAEA was designed to promote Eisenhower’s “atoms for peace” or the peaceful use of nuclear power, technology and medicine for developmental purposes. Indeed, under the aegis of Upendra Lal Goswami, the first and to date only Indian Deputy Director General of the IAEA in the 1960s and 1970s, the technical assistance programme of the IAEA grew and flourished. Whilst the IAEA continued to undertake the selective use of safeguards policing of non-nuclear weapons states, the objective was that in exchange for such safeguards inspections, non-nuclear weapons states would be allowed to develop peaceful uses of nuclear power with the support and assistance of the IAEA.
To further undergird this two-track system on nuclear arms, the Treaty on Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) was opened for signature in 1968, and it entered into force in 1970 and was extended indefinitely in 1995. To date, 191 countries have signed the NPT, including the five original nuclear weapons states and 186 non-nuclear weapons states.
Is NPT in its current form preventing conflict?
It could be argued that considering these many signatures, the global community of nations has made NPT customary international law. Advocates could point to NPT’s success in South Africa, which under the ANC, post the fall of the apartheid regime, abandoned the secret nuclear weapons programme it had been developing with Western support to usher in a nuclear weapon free zone in Africa. This appears to advance the argument that the current NPT prevents the devastating consequences of nuclear war.
Yet, it is evident that universal nuclear disarmament under the NPT is impossible because the P5 have steadfastly refused to disarm, even though Article VI commits every party to pursue negotiations in good faith on nuclear disarmament. In addition, some states have refused to accept NPT or withdrew from it. India, Pakistan, Israel and South Sudan did not sign the NPT. North Korea, which acceded to NPT in 1985, announced its withdrawal in 2003. Critics of NPT could argue that those states that did not sign the NPT or withdrew from it avoided large scale and prolonged regional conflict, whereas states that did sign NPT have become subject to major regional conflicts.
In South Asia, both India and Pakistan, after refusing to sign the NPT, have become nuclear weapons states. Since then, even though their conflicts have remained frequent, they are more limited in scope than the large-scale conventional wars common before the early 1970s, partly because of the risk of mutually assured destruction.
In addition to this, India accepted the idea of selective safeguards inspections by the IAEA. As part of a historic deal enabling India to obtain a waiver from the Nuclear Suppliers Group in 2008 for nuclear commerce, notwithstanding not signing the NPT, India agreed to selective inspection of designated civilian nuclear facilities under a specific safeguards agreement (INFCIRC/754). This arrangement did not require inspections of India’s entire nuclear programme, including military facilities, as would have been required under the NPT. India also signed an Additional Protocol to expand the scope of IAEA inspection to certain declared nuclear materials and components.
Meanwhile, North and South Korea were engaged in a large-scale conflict in the 1950s backed by foreign powers, such as the US and China. The development of a nuclear programme by North Korea meant that it could negotiate with South Korea and South Korea’s allies in the 1990s and 2000s, in exchange for sanctions relief. Since then, there has been no large-scale conventional conflict. Today, there is a stalemate basis the possession of nuclear weapons by North Korea.
In contrast to South Asia and the Korean Peninsula, the Middle East has been embroiled in a long and painful regional conflict. Unlike the nuclear weapons induced stalemate on large-scale conventional wars in South Asia and the Korean Peninsula, Israel has adopted a policy of strategic ambiguity on possession of nuclear weapons and has refused to sign the NPT. Yet Iran, which has been in conflict with Israel, is being asked to abide strictly by the NPT and abjure nuclear weapons. Given the lack of a nuclear deterrent, Iran has opted for closure or blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and has extended the conflict to UAE and Saudi Arabia with disastrous consequences for especially the Global South.
What about the Ukraine-Russia conflict? As the Soviet Union collapsed, the European powers, led by the United Kingdom (UK), supported the United States in pushing for Ukraine’s nuclear disarmament, which culminated in the signing of the so-called Budapest Memorandum of December 1994, under which Ukraine relinquished the world’s third largest arsenal of nuclear weapons of over 1,700 nuclear warheads in exchange for economic assistance and its sovereignty. In short, the UK, with nuclear weapons of its own, and the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) states, under a nuclear weapons umbrella, pushed Ukraine to undergo nuclear disarmament. This raises the question: would Russia have invaded Ukraine in 2022 if it still had nuclear weapons?
A comparative history of regional conflicts suggests that the 1950s global order of a limited number of nuclear weapons states, reflected in the NPT of 1968, has come to an end. Further, countries that have been invaded may be drawing the lesson that lack of access to nuclear weapons leads to such invasion and large-scale conventional conflict, thereby increasing the likely move towards nuclear arms. These developments suggest that the risks of nuclear war and conventional conflict are increasing and not decreasing under the current NPT framework, underscoring the urgent need for its bold reimagining.
NPT 2.0: The way forward
The Global South is most impacted by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Also, the new geopolitical reality of “might is right” among major powers could trigger untrammeled nuclear proliferation if the NPT is left in its current outdated form. articles.summary: India, Israel vote against Pakistan-Belarus resolution on regional arms control at UN; New Delhi explains  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
Listen to this article in summarized format
The draft resolution, titled ‘General and complete disarmament: Conventional arms control at the regional and subregional levels’, was adopted by the UN General Assembly's First Committee on Monday, with 180 members voting in favour, two against and none abstaining. India and Israel were the only two countries to oppose the proposal in the 193-member UN body.
Explaining India's position, Anmol Sher Bedi, First Secretary at India's Permanent Mission to the UN, said conventional arms control was a global issue and should not be pursued primarily through regional and subregional frameworks.
New Delhi voted against the draft in line with its established position on the subject, Bedi said while delivering India's explanation of vote before the First Committee.
Also Read: Watch video: How the Indian Navy freed hijacked fishing vessel Azini and rescued all 20 crew members in a 48-hour operation in the Arabian Sea
India questions fresh UN deliberations on conventional arms control
Bedi also raised objections to a provision asking the UN Disarmament Commission to consider developing principles that could form the basis for regional agreements on conventional arms control.
New Delhi says security concerns extend beyond regional boundaries
India also disagreed with the resolution's emphasis on maintaining a balance in defence capabilities within individual regions or subregions.
Bedi argued that such an approach assumed countries' security concerns were confined to the geographical regions they belonged to, which was not the case. He said these concerns extended beyond narrowly defined regional boundaries and described the idea of preserving a military balance within a particular region or subregion as unrealistic.
The Pakistan-Belarus draft argued that conventional arms control should primarily be pursued at regional and subregional levels because most threats to peace and security in the post-Cold War period arise among countries located within the same region.
It also called for agreements that would strengthen regional peace and security while keeping armaments and military forces at the lowest possible levels. The resolution further stated that militarily significant countries and those with greater military capabilities had a special responsibility to promote such arrangements.
India separately opposes reference to South Asian arms control proposals
Apart from voting against the overall resolution, India also opposed a separate paragraph referring to conventional arms control proposals made in the context of South Asia.
The paragraph expressed particular interest in initiatives undertaken in different regions, including consultations among some Latin American countries and proposals for conventional arms control in South Asia. It also acknowledged the relevance of conventional arms control to regional security.
India's opposition to this provision was in line with its broader objections to treating arms control primarily through regional frameworks, as outlined by Bedi during the explanation of vote.

articles.title: The Missing Critical Minerals Investment
articles.summary: To catch up to China, America and its allies must dig.
articles.full_text:
The United States and its allies are finally taking supply chains for critical minerals seriously. China has spent the last three decades building a dominant share of global mineral production, and the export controls Beijing has introduced periodically since 2023 have made clear just how dangerous it is for other countries to rely on China for access to materials that are essential components of semiconductors, defense technologies, and automobiles.
Washington and European capitals are now trying to minimize their exposure. Alongside private firms, these governments have begun investing in both upstream industries including mines, refineries, and recycling infrastructure and downstream industries such as magnets and batteries. The bulk of their efforts so far have focused on mines already in operation or close to it and on refining. It is true that the United States and Europe do not have sufficient facilities to process raw ore into specialized chemicals or refined materials and that building more refining facilities will help reduce their reliance on China and alleviate immediate supply chain concerns.
But this is a temporary fix. Refining facilities are valuable only if they have a steady, long-term supply of raw materials. That, in turn, requires new mines, especially as advanced industries demand ever more minerals. Because building a mine takes roughly 20 years, ensuring a long-term supply of minerals requires investing in new mines now. China, which is committed to maintaining its supply chain dominance, has been willing to allocate substantial capital to such ventures. Japan has, too, ever since China blocked exports of critical minerals to the country amid a dispute over the Senkaku Islands (known in China as the Diaoyu Islands) in 2010, which pushed Tokyo to start the long process of disentangling its own supply chains. But Japan still has a long way to go; after 15 years of investing, the country has reduced its dependence on China for rare earths from about 90 percent to between 65 and 70 percent—not nearly enough to supply its own needs, much less those of its allies.
In short, investing in refining is necessary but insufficient. To avoid future supply chain vulnerabilities, the United States and its allies, especially those in the G-7, must also start building a pipeline of new mines. These investments are long bets, and they are risky. But when successful, they reap high rewards.
THE VALLEY OF DEATH
The United States and its allies significantly outperform China in mineral exploration. Australian and Canadian firms alone account for roughly one-third of global exploration spending. But the vast majority of geological prospects never become operating mines. This is not for lack of financing in prospecting but because of the many financial disincentives and risks that appear once a mining project moves forward.
The initial stages of mining development rely chiefly on a unique ecosystem of mining companies called “juniors,” so called because they have a small market cap, focus exclusively on one or a few projects, and are nowhere large enough to list on major stock exchanges. Most of them list in Australia or Canada and concentrate on the initial high-risk exploration stages. Geological uncertainty makes betting on junior ventures extraordinarily risky, but if a mineral deposit proves to have significant reserves, the junior can sell the project or bring in a new partner, and that payout is large.
Yet in the next stages, investors tend to lose patience or run out of capital. Although initial prospecting is relatively cheap, subsequent feasibility studies that estimate a deposit’s size, engineering needs, costs, and expected returns can easily run into the tens of millions of dollars, in addition to the costs of drilling, engineering, permitting, and development planning. Commercial lenders stay away because these projects have no immediate revenue, no assets to offer as collateral, and no guarantees they will even be viable. The risk, in short, is too high to take for uncertain returns. Large mining companies also avoid these projects because they face pressure from shareholders to provide maximum returns. Even as demand for minerals has risen, the share of revenue that major mining companies have reinvested in new development has stayed flat.
Without outside financing, juniors cannot complete the studies needed to attract additional financing for construction, even if they have found a promising deposit. As single-asset companies, they have no other cash flow or assets to offer as collateral for additional loans. This moment is often referred to as the “valley of death.” Many companies looking for a way out of this predicament have turned to one reliable source of investment: China. Chinese companies are much more willing to take on this type of risk and provide the necessary capital to advance mining projects, and they are often the only viable option for juniors. Thus, China’s dominance in global supply chains relies on Western companies’ exploration. It endures not because China offers more competitive terms but because at a key financing stage, it is the only game in town.
DOWNSTREAM EFFECTS
China has been expanding its supply pipeline for critical minerals for decades. In 2025, it spent a record $32 billion on metals and mining projects through its Belt and Road Initiative, breaking the previous year’s record of $21 billion. Chinese firms are also willing to invest in equity, buying ownership stakes in companies that come with no guaranteed returns. Additional spending takes the form of resources-for-infrastructure deals, by which China funds infrastructure such as ports, energy facilities, and railways in mineral-rich countries in exchange for a share in the profits of mining projects—which Chinese companies and state banks may also help finance. By investing in a broad portfolio of mineral projects across several countries, Chinese firms can let the profits of those that succeed cover the losses of those that fail.
Apart from capital, the most important part of China’s mining strategy is know-how. Because failure is so common, the ability to identify deposits with the highest potential to deliver is crucial. Beijing relies on specialized state-owned enterprises, geological firms, private companies, and government officials to vet projects and work with host governments to secure permits, infrastructure, and delivery. The only G-7 country that maintains a comparable on-the-ground presence for mining projects is Japan, in countries such as Australia, Canada, Peru, and Uzbekistan. These projects are intended to secure critical minerals that can support Japan’s industries, but they are currently insufficient to meet all of Japan’s production needs, let alone broader allied needs.
The disparity between China’s mining investments and those of the United States and its allies is most evident in Africa, home to some of the largest untapped mineral resources. Whereas the United States invested about $300 million in critical mineral projects on the continent in 2023, China invested about $8 billion to $10 billion. Washington has recognized the need to close this gap, but it still has a long way to go.
In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, a particular focus of the Trump administration, Chinese companies control about 70 percent of cobalt and copper mines. Between 2008 and 2020, Chinese banks and companies extended over $9 billion in credit for mine development and operations in Congo, in addition to $3 billion in infrastructure loans from the Export-Import Bank of China. The United States and other G-7 countries had the opportunity to take part in these investments but judged the projects to be too risky. In 2015, for example, the Canadian-listed mining company Ivanhoe Mines sought funding for its Kamoa-Kakula copper project in Congo. With no Western investors willing to take on the risk, the Chinese firm Zijin Mining acquired an ownership stake. Today, Kamoa-Kakula is on track to become one of the largest copper mines in the world. Meanwhile, in 2016 and 2020, the only major American mining company active in Congo sold its stakes in two substantial copper-cobalt deposits, its only remaining stakes in the country, to a Chinese mining company.
The owners of a mine control where its minerals eventually go. When Chinese firms own a mine, the output flows either to their refineries or downstream manufacturers in China. The Chinese battery giant CATL, for example, has an ownership stake in the Kisanfu mine in Congo, where it secures a steady supply of copper and cobalt for its batteries. U.S. automakers and allied battery producers have also invested in some projects, but none to the same degree—even still, much of that material flows through China. The concentration of this refined material in China gives Beijing ever-greater market power and the ability to weaponize it.
MINING THE SOLUTION
In theory, the United States and its allies have the means of financing their own pipeline of future mining projects. In 2024, two Toronto-based stock exchanges hosted nearly 1,100 publicly listed mining companies, 40 percent of the global total. These companies account for roughly one-third of the world’s total mining equity capital raised over the last five years. About half of the listed companies’ projects were based in Canada. The Australian Stock Exchange is another key exchange, with about 850 companies listed in 2024 for mining development.

articles.title: The Fight for the Future of Democratic Foreign Policy
articles.summary: Which debates matter most for 2028.
articles.full_text:
The midterm elections mark the beginning of the Democratic Party’s 2028 presidential campaign. After two years of debate over the lessons of Kamala Harris’s defeat in the 2024 election, it promises to be one of the most open contests about the future of Democratic policies, including foreign policy, in generations. It also promises to be one of the most consequential. The strategic environment in 2029 is on track to be the most difficult and unforgiving since the height of the Cold War.
Democrats must therefore lay out their ideas early and see how they fare both with voters and against the trajectory of world events. The party is generally split into two camps: centrists who, when it comes to foreign policy, are focused on strategic competition, restoring the United States’ national power, and deepening alliances; and progressives, who propose a more affirmative agenda emphasizing shared challenges and global cooperation. In many ways, this divide has become familiar. But as the second Trump administration continues its project of overturning the post–World War II global order, the debates within each camp are at least as important as the disagreements between them.
If the party’s major foreign policy disagreements—on the future of the international order, on Israel, on artificial intelligence, on China, and on the global economy—are not litigated by prospective candidates, former officials, and prominent thinkers now, and voters are not given the chance to make an informed choice between coherent options, the first year of a Democratic administration could be consumed by indecision and infighting. Democrats must therefore understand where they stand on each of those questions, where centrists and progressives converge, and where the sharpest divisions now lie.
AFTER BIDEN
The three Democratic presidents since the end of the Cold War have all made some version of a U.S.-led international order a cornerstone of their foreign policy. But although former President Joe Biden’s rhetoric, with its emblematic “America Is Back” catchphrase, gestured at restoring that order after Trump, Biden did not govern like a restorationist. For the Biden administration, in which I served, the intensifying strategic competition with China and Russia and the onset of shared challenges such as the pandemic marked an external unraveling of the old era that necessitated major changes in U.S. strategy. Biden shifted foreign economic policy away from free trade and globalization toward industrial policy, resilience, and technological leadership, and he pushed back more assertively against Beijing and Moscow than did his Democratic predecessors.
As they reflect on the Biden administration, centrists are actively debating whether a future Democratic administration can restore and reform the U.S.-led international order or whether the United States must adapt to a prolonged period of geopolitical upheaval. For now, the differences are more pronounced in diagnosis than in policy prescriptions. All favor deepening alliances and partnerships, modernizing the military, fixing the defense industrial base, strengthening deterrence, tackling transnational challenges such as global public health, and pursuing hardheaded diplomacy with rivals.
Centrists also agree that Trump has severely weakened U.S. power and institutions, although they remain relatively optimistic about the country’s capacity to recover. But most recognize that the world the next Democratic president would inherit in 2029 is not the world that Biden inherited in 2021. Winning an election will not mean the end of Trumpism. The “America first” movement will likely remain a dominant force in the Republican Party, and the United States’ allies and partners will have to hedge against dramatic shifts in U.S. foreign policy from one election to the next. Even if a Democratic president can rebuild American power and repair damaged institutions, restoring international confidence in the durability of U.S. commitments will be much harder.
 Winning an election will not mean the end of Trumpism.
The party’s progressives argue that the U.S. foreign policy establishment failed over the past 25 years by pursuing U.S. primacy at all costs. They see the U.S.-led order as deeply flawed in its design and track record, arguing that Washington’s selective application of the “rules-based order” undermined the order itself. As Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, of New York, put it at the Munich Security Conference in 2026, “In a rules-based order, hypocrisy is vulnerability.” They favor a rules-based order that applies its principles consistently, even if doing so constrains the United States.
Many progressives, led by Bernie Sanders, the independent senator from Vermont, also believe that a global oligarchy poses a threat to democracy and see big business in defense, technology, and finance as part of a corrupt system. They believe that corporate interests have driven excessive military spending, misguided interventions, and a global economy that favors multinational companies over workers.
Progressives see the turmoil of the past two years as accelerating the emergence of a multipolar order, in which the United States has an important, but more limited, role to play. According to the progressive thinker Ben Rhodes, a former deputy national security adviser to President Barack Obama, Washington should “re-engage the world as something other than a hegemon.” Americans are accustomed to seeing the country as an overall force for good, even when it uses military power, but progressives point to U.S. support for Israel’s war in Gaza, and the Trump administration’s actions in Iran and Venezuela as evidence of the enormous damage that interventionism can cause. Many argue that the United States should go to war only in self-defense—and with congressional authorization, as the Constitution requires. They also favor cuts to what they see as a bloated defense budget that encourages presidents to default to military action instead of diplomacy.
 New debates, both between and within the various camps of the Democratic Party, are emerging.
Most progressives believe that the greatest threats to American security and prosperity are increasingly transnational rather than geopolitical: runaway artificial intelligence, climate change, and widening inequality, as enumerated by Sanders earlier this year. They argue that the threat from China is often overblown and that deterrence can be achieved and U.S. interests protected with existing capabilities and without a ratcheting up of tensions. As such, most progressives would prioritize cooperation with other powers, especially Beijing, on existential challenges over competition.
A distinct group of thinkers, usually aligned with the progressive camp, identifies with the restraint school of foreign policy. They tend to agree with the centrists about the centrality of geopolitics but want to reduce the United States’ exposure to it. They argue that Washington’s pursuit of military primacy has overstretched the country, unnecessarily embroiling it in conflicts and crises, and favor a more selective approach that focuses on a smaller number of vital interests, reduces overseas commitments, and emphasizes diplomacy, even if it leads to outcomes abroad that conflict with their values.
Despite these differing worldviews, there is much agreement between centrists and progressives. Both camps support NATO, the EU, and Washington’s alliances in the Indo-Pacific. Both want to stand up to Russian President Vladimir Putin and help Ukraine. Both oppose the Iran war and both want to root out corruption. But new debates, both between and within the various camps of the Democratic Party, are steadily emerging alongside those that have historically divided the party.
SHOCK OF THE NEW
One of the most important debates currently unfolding in the party is the United States’ relationship with Israel and Washington’s role in the Middle East more generally. This is likely to be the most pronounced break from the Biden administration. articles.title: What Sanctions Get Right
articles.summary: A useful tool has been unjustly maligned.
articles.full_text:
The United States frequently uses sanctions or embargoes to rein in malign actors. When policymakers become dissatisfied with the results, they often embrace military action next. Washington, for example, applied sanctions on Iraq for more than a decade before invading the country in 2003. It did the same with Iran, using sanctions to pressure the government into nuclear negotiations in the 2010s and then, after withdrawing from the resulting agreement in 2018, going to war with Tehran in February 2026.
Washington follows this pattern of behavior because sanctions alone rarely—if ever—make a problem disappear, such as by toppling the government responsible. This frustrates Americans, who tend to seek simple, quick, and permanent fixes to foreign policy problems. Many interpret the persistence of these problems as evidence that sanctions are futile. But the effectiveness of sanctions is measured in crises that do not occur—the nuclear test that never happens, for instance, or the shipping lane that remains undisturbed. These successes are invisible, but an adversary’s continuing provocations are not. As a result, American officials often conclude that it is necessary to turn to war.
This logic reflects a misunderstanding about how sanctions work. Sanctions may not be able to achieve maximalist aims, yet when they are deployed in concert with other policy tools, they can help manage problems. They do this by reliably depressing the target country’s economic growth over time. Although this hurts innocent civilians in the targeted countries as their leaders shift the costs from regime supporters to the politically disenfranchised, no government can escape the inexorable math of slowing economic growth. If an economy starts out with a three percent growth rate—roughly the global average—it will double in size in around 23 years. But if sanctions reduce annual growth to one percent, doubling in size will take 70 years, three times as long. Just compare the North Korean and South Korean economies, or look at nighttime satellite imagery of the Korean Peninsula, to see the compounding effects of sanctions over generations. Although sanctions may not change the targeted regime’s aspirations, they reduce its financial wherewithal and may deter other governments from emulating the behavior that precipitated the sanctions.
Wars can overthrow adversarial regimes, but usually only after years of fighting, and fixing the damage afterward takes considerable time and money. Too often the United States misidentifies its foreign policy problems as solvable on the cheap. It took an Allied occupation force of over 1.5 million soldiers to garrison Germany, a country of 80 million, after World War II. Fast forward 60 years, and Washington was not interested in raising the numbers of troops necessary to subdue Iraq, a country of nearly 30 million. Americans today are likewise unwilling to make sacrifices on the scale necessary to vanquish Iran, with its 90 million people—much less China, with its 1.4 billion. The challenges these countries might pose are too large to solve at an acceptable cost. In such cases, sanctions offer an economically sustainable strategy to manage troublesome situations in the long term.
THE FIRST MISTAKE
According to the conventional wisdom about sanctions, these measures discourage unsavory behavior by raising its economic costs. If force becomes necessary, they also weaken the adversary in advance of war. This logic has endured since 1935, when the League of Nations sanctioned Italy for invading Ethiopia, in the hope that doing so would induce Italy to call off its invasion or at least temper its ambitions. Yet because the countries imposing sanctions were unwilling to include vital commodities such as oil and coal on the list of sanctioned items, the effort was ineffective.
Sanctions have evolved since 1935. Today, unlike broad sanctions that inflict significant collateral damage, so-called smart sanctions target specific institutions or individuals and are enforced through the banking system, blocking financial transactions linked to sanctioned activities. UN sanctions against Iraq starting in 1990 were, in a sense, the last gasp of the old sanctions regime. Their lifting was contingent on Iraq’s dismantling its weapons of mass destruction program and agreeing to respect Kuwaiti sovereignty. Because verification of the former proved difficult, many of the sanctions remained in place after a 1991 armistice, and they continued through the 2003 Iraq war. After U.S.-led forces invaded Iraq in March 2003 and overthrew Saddam Hussein, it became apparent that the sanctions had been effective. Isolation from the global economy had prevented Iraq from restoring its economy, rebuilding its military, and resuming its development of weapons of mass destruction.
Between the two wars, however, many observers believed that international sanctions were unable to deter Iraqi aggression and neutralize its weapons programs. Worried that Iraq’s Sunni government still posed a threat to Kurds in the north and Shiites in the south, the United States, the United Kingdom, and, for a short time, France imposed two no-fly zones over those regions, without UN consent. In 1998, after Baghdad expelled UN weapons inspectors, the United States and the United Kingdom bombed Iraq. The same year, a group of hawkish scholars and former government officials sent an open letter to U.S. President Bill Clinton describing the sanctions-based Iraq policy as “dangerously inadequate.” Many of these signatories would return to government in the George W. Bush administration to implement their recommendations.
To a certain extent, the critics had a point. Political divisions within the United States and between Washington and its partners had constrained international efforts to contain Saddam. Arab governments may have been wary of hurting their relationships with the United States, but Arab publics were sick of Western imperialism. The growing U.S. military presence in the Middle East further antagonized both the anti-imperialist left and radical Islamists, and many Europeans resented American unilateralism.
 No government can escape the inexorable math of slowing economic growth.
Saddam also pushed doctored stories about civilian hardship arising from sanctions, which Western journalists readily covered. Iraqi suffering was very real, but it was largely a result of Saddam’s own policies, which channeled resources to his regime rather than to the civilian population. Starting in 1995, the UN’s oil-for-food program allowed Iraq to sell some oil to pay for civilian necessities, but Saddam used the profits to pay kickbacks instead. He signed lucrative oil deals with China, France, and Russia, enticing these permanent UN Security Council members to weaken their support for sanctions. It was around this time that the UN and civil society groups started calling for smart sanctions, to narrow the scope of economic punishment and avoid causing wide-scale economic pain, although it would take several more years for the United States to refine this tool.
In the meantime, in Iraq, sanctions and no-fly-zone enforcement became increasingly frustrating, costly, and unpopular. Because their main purpose was to prevent Iraq from developing weapons of mass destruction and funding malign activities such as international terrorism, they required constant vigilance. Then came the 9/11 attacks and the war in Afghanistan, where a U.S.-led coalition toppled the Taliban regime within months, suggesting that wars—at least those conducted by the highly trained, technologically advanced U.S. military—could solve problems, unlike the sanctions that left dictators in place.
When U.S. President George W. Bush announced the Iraq war on March 19, 2003, he described its goals as “to disarm Iraq, to free its people, and to defend the world from grave danger.” This danger was Iraq’s alleged stockpiles of weapons of mass destruction and its links to al-Qaeda, the group behind 9/11. At first, Washington intended to leave the task of reconstructing Iraq to the UN, but it had to abandon that strategy five months after the invasion when foreign jihadists bombed the UN’s local headquarters, killing the head of the mission and 22 others. Within weeks, the UN withdrew most of its 600 staff members, leaving the United States fully in charge.
Rather than ending the trouble Iraq caused, occupation created more problems. The war lent credence to al-Qaeda’s accusations that Washington oppressed Muslims, attracting would-be jihadists around the world to join the cause. In 2006, al-Qaeda’s bombing of the Golden Mosque in Samarra, a holy site for Shiites, triggered brutal Sunni–Shiite fighting. More than 4,000 Americans lost their lives over the course of the war, while more than 200,000 Iraqis lost theirs. After the U.S. withdrawal in 2011, much of the Middle East and North Africa went up in flames. Foreign jihadists and remnants of Saddam’s Baath Party formed the Islamic State, also known as ISIS, and overran much of Iraq and Syria in 2014 and 2015. U.S.- and Iranian-backed forces gradually and at great cost pushed the group out, but many of its fighters simply took up arms elsewhere. Some went to Sahelian Africa, exacerbating violence there. Others joined the opposition to Bashar al-Assad’s regime in Syria. And the refugee crisis sparked in part by the Islamic State’s initial expansion continues to roil Europe.
Whereas war brought spiraling instability to the Middle East, North Africa, and Europe, international sanctions were more effective than U.S. policymakers thought. While they were in place, Iraq was unable to build weapons of mass destruction, and it dismantled many of its existing programs to secure sanctions relief.
